title: Prompt, Check, Publish
text:
Preface: How to Use This Book
Change one number in a dataset, and how many documents are now wrong? If the number was copied by hand into a report, a slide, an email and a web page, nobody knows without searching. This book teaches a way of publishing with nothing to search for: you write once, in plain text, and a web page, a Word document, a PDF, slides, an e-book, a website, a blog and a dashboard all rebuild from that one source with one command. The program that rebuilds them is Quarto.
Quarto is one of three parts. With git, which records every version of the source, and a hosting service such as GitHub Pages, which puts the result on the web, it lets one person produce reproducible, publication-quality work for a wide range of settings and formats: a page read on a phone, a report printed for a meeting, slides on a projector, an e-book, an interactive dashboard. Coding assistants speed all of it up. The cryptic commands and fragile configuration that used to stand between an analysis and its published, interactive form are no longer the bottleneck: you describe the step, the assistant writes the commands, and you check the result.

title: Prompt, Check, Publish
text:
Prompt, Check, Publish
The title names the method, a loop you run at every step of both projects. You prompt a coding assistant, a program that writes files and runs commands at your request, describing one small piece of work with its files and columns named. You check what it did: read what changed, look at the result, compare it with the data. An assistant can be fluent, fast and wrong, so this step is never skipped, and it is always yours. Then Quarto publishes, rebuilding every output from the checked source the same way every time. Chapter 1 explains why the last step can be trusted, and Chapter 2 how to make the first two reliable.
Every hands-on step in Parts II and III goes once round the loop in Figure 1.






Figure 1: Prompt, Check, Publish: the loop this book teaches, with who acts at each step.

title: Prompt, Check, Publish
text:
Who this book is for
I wrote this book for researchers, software practitioners, data experts and students: anyone who works with data/code and needs to share the results. It shows how to publish from one source of plain-text file (prose & code), using Quarto. Quarto is free and open source traditional software, so every report, slide deck and web page is reproducible, interactive and of publication quality. With a coding assistant, work that once took days now takes minutes. Along the way, I explain the concepts, arguments and decisions behind each step.
Reproducibility is why I wrote this book. Work that others can rebuild earns their trust, justifies the decisions made on it, and gives them something to build on, which is how science, technology and understanding move forward. More automation means fewer errors and a better experience, for the people who make the work and for those who read it.
Publishing is half the job; the other half is being read. Content works only if it engages the people it is for, so the book treats every output as something a particular reader will use, and checks it as that reader would. My hope is that it improves the interactions, and the outcomes, of everyone who works with data, software and AI applications and has to communicate them.
You may be new to Quarto, to coding assistants or to both. No programming is assumed: I explain the Python the assistant writes, but you do not have to write it. If the terminal is new to you, Chapter 3 teaches the little you need, one checked step at a time.
You will need a computer on which you can install software (Windows, Mac or Linux), a free GitHub account, and an account with one coding assistant (Before you start lists what each needs).

The two running examples
Every concept is tied to one of two projects, both built on real, cited data.
A London visitor guide (Part II). For the city’s tourism office, you write one guide that becomes a web page, a Word brief for partners, a printed flyer, a dashboard for managers and a published website. Every visitor number in it, from the 7,116,929 visits to the Natural History Museum (South Kensington) in 2025 down, is computed from the counts published by the Association of Leading Visitor Attractions.
Drinking-water risk in Colombian municipalities (Part III). You group Colombia’s municipal zones into kinds by water safety, services and context, from 2016 to 2023, compare health and education outcomes between the kinds, and publish the analysis as a report, slides, a blog post and a website, all from one analysis script. Most of the data are Colombian open data, joined by official municipality codes; rainfall comes from the Climate Hazards Center’s CHIRPS data and altitude from NASA’s SRTM elevation data (Appendix G — Data Sources, Licences and Credits).

The assistant reports a render with no errors. Is the work checked?

When you get stuck
You will get stuck: an install fails, a prompt goes wrong, a render stops with an error you have never seen. That is expected, and the book is built for it. Every hands-on block ends at a checkpoint, a folder in the workshop’s repository (checkpoints/), the copy of the workshop’s files you download during setup (Step 5: Run the setup check). It holds the project as it should be at that point, with a README listing the steps to catch up. The rule is simple: stuck for two minutes, catch up. Where the book reaches a checkpoint, a catch-up box gives the one line to paste into your assistant (Figure 2).






Figure 2: Catching up from a checkpoint. Your work is backed up first, so nothing is lost.



The README’s last step names the workshop slide to rejoin at. In the book, that place is the catch-up box itself, so after catching up you carry on reading from the box. If you were stuck partway through a block, go straight to its box: the checkpoint already holds the steps between where you stopped and the box. Appendix E — Checkpoints at a Glance, and Answers lists every checkpoint.

Three chapters stand between you and the first project: one for the Publish step of the loop, one for Prompt and Check, and one for the machine that runs them all.
Chapter 1, Publishing That Rebuilds Itself. Why hand-made reports drift out of date, and how Quarto rebuilds every output from one source so that they cannot. title: 1  Publishing That Rebuilds Itself
text:
1.1 Why reports drift
Most reports are built by hand. An analyst runs a script, copies a number into a Word document, pastes a chart into a slide, retypes the same number in an email, and exports a PDF for the website. Every copy is a small act of faith that the number was right and is still right. When the data change, someone has to find every copy, and nobody can say for sure where each one came from.
That faith is the problem, because the reason to publish data is that people rely on it. Work that can be reproduced earns trust: a reader, a reviewer or a manager can see where each number came from, and rebuild it. It justifies decisions, because the evidence behind a choice can be shown, checked again and defended later. And it can be built on: someone else starts from your source rather than from scratch, extends it and corrects it, which is how science, technology and understanding improve. Work that cannot be reproduced offers none of this; it asks to be taken on trust.
The alternative is one source that rebuilds every output, the Publish step of this book’s loop. The more of that work a program does, the fewer places an error can slip in, and the better the experience for everyone involved: the people who make the documents, and the people who read documents that agree with each other and with the data.
The London visitor guide that runs through Part II is a small example of a common problem. The tourism office publishes the same facts to several audiences: a web guide for visitors, a dashboard for managers, a Word brief for partners, a square social-media card and, later, a white paper. In the finished project, five pages read the same table of attraction visits, and between them they write ten files: the guide alone becomes a web page, a Word document, a PDF, a PowerPoint deck, an e-book and a slide deck that runs in the browser.
Suppose the Association of Leading Visitor Attractions (ALVA), the source of those counts, corrects one figure. In a copy-and-paste workflow, that correction has to reach ten files by hand. Three things tend to go wrong:
None of these is a failure of care. They are what happens when the output is treated as the thing you edit. The fix is structural: edit the source, and let a program rebuild the outputs (Figure 1.1).

title: 1  Publishing That Rebuilds Itself
text:
1.2 What Quarto is
Quarto is an open-source publishing system, free for anyone to use: a command-line program, one you run by typing a command in a terminal (Section 3.3), that turns plain-text source files into finished documents.
The input is either a plain Markdown file (.md) or a Quarto document (.qmd). Markdown is a way of writing structured text with a few punctuation marks, such as # before a heading (Chapter 4). A .qmd file is Markdown with two additions: a block of settings at the top, written in YAML, a format for settings in which indentation is meaning (Section 5.1), and code cells, fenced blocks of code that run when the document is built. Here is a complete one, the file the test run in Chapter 3 asks your assistant to write:
---
title: "Hello"
format:
  html: default
  typst: default
---

```{python}
answer = 6 * 7
```

The answer is `{python} answer`.
Between the two --- lines are the settings: a title and two formats, a web page (html) and a PDF (typst). The fenced block below them is a code cell. The sentence at the bottom contains inline code: when the document is built, Quarto runs answer and writes its value into the sentence. When this book was built, the same calculation gave 42, and that number was computed, not typed.

1.2.1 Three steps: execute, convert, typeset
To render a document is to build its outputs from its source, and quarto render does it in three steps (Figure 1.2).






Figure 1.2: What quarto render does. One source becomes Markdown with results, which Pandoc converts to each output format; for PDF, Typst typesets the result.




Execute. A computation engine runs the code cells: Jupyter for Python, knitr for R. The results (numbers, tables, figures) replace the code in an intermediate Markdown file. The cells run once for each format, so each output gets results made for it (Section 5.5). This book uses Python only.
Convert. For each format, Pandoc, a long-established document converter, reads that Markdown and writes the output: HTML, Word (docx), EPUB, PowerPoint (pptx) or a Reveal.js slide deck.
Typeset. For PDF, Pandoc writes source for Typst, a modern typesetting system that ships inside Quarto, and Typst produces the PDF. No LaTeX installation is needed. (Quarto can also make PDFs through LaTeX, format: pdf, if you install a TeX distribution.)

The split matters in practice. A failure in step 1 is a failure of your code: a missing package, a wrong column name, a cell that raises an error. A failure in step 2 or 3 is a failure of the document: a malformed table, an image too large for the page, a format-specific option that does not exist. When a render fails, the error message tells you which step stopped, and that tells you where to look.


Pause and think


A render of london.qmd stops with KeyError: 'visits_2025'. Which step failed, and where do you look first?



Answer

Step 1, execute. A code cell asked the data for a column it does not have, so compare the cell with the column names in the data file. The format settings are not the problem: Pandoc and Typst never ran.








NoteWhy this works



Pandoc converts between many formats by reading every input into one internal document model and writing every output from that model. That is why one Markdown file can become both a Word document and a slide deck: neither output is derived from the other. Both come from the same kind of structured intermediate, built from the same source, so a heading is a heading everywhere.

The official list of formats is long and grouped by kind (Quarto, All Formats, checked 2026-11-12):

title: 1  Publishing That Rebuilds Itself
text:
1.3 Quarto is not AI
This book pairs Quarto with a coding assistant, and the pairing invites a misunderstanding: that Quarto itself is an AI tool. It is not. Quarto is conventional software. Given the same source files and the same data, it writes the same outputs every time. It does not generate text, code or figures of its own, and it sends nothing to an AI service.
The assistant is a separate program. It reads and writes the files in your project folder and runs commands you approve; Quarto then turns those files into formats. The two have different failure modes, and the workflow in this book is designed around the difference:



Table 1.2: Two tools with different failure modes.











Coding assistant
Quarto




Output for the same input
varies from run to run
identical


Typical mistake
plausible but wrong code or prose
a precise, reproducible error


How you check it
read its changes, run them, compare with the data
read the rendered output






Because generation and rendering are separate, every mistake the assistant makes lands in a file you can read or a command you approve before anything is published: that gap is where the Check step of the loop happens. And because the render is repeatable, anyone can rebuild your outputs to confirm them, without trusting the assistant at all.


Pause and think


Asked twice for the same chart, the assistant writes two different code cells. If you keep one and render it twice, do you get two different charts?



Answer

No. The assistant varies; Quarto does not. Once the cell is in the file, every render runs the same code on the same data, so you check the cell once and every rebuild inherits that check.








WarningCommon pitfall



Quarto runs whatever code your cells contain. If a cell calls an AI service, the document becomes as unpredictable as that service, and the cause is your code, not Quarto. Keep calls to models out of rendered documents unless the variation is the point.

title: 1  Publishing That Rebuilds Itself
text:
1.4 Reproducible: same source, same result
Reproducible is used loosely, so here is the precise sense this book means: someone else, or you in six months, can rebuild the same results from the same files with one command, and can see where every number came from. Four properties make that possible:
One source. Text, code and data live in plain files in one folder. Nothing important exists only inside an application.
Numbers are computed. Every figure, table and number in a sentence comes from a code cell or inline code that reads the data. Nothing is typed in or pasted from elsewhere.
One command. quarto render rebuilds everything. There is no sequence of manual export steps to remember.
Versioned. Git, the version-control tool installed in Chapter 3, is something like Word’s Track Changes for a whole folder, with a lasting history; a project folder with its history is a repository. Each state of the source, data and settings that you choose to record becomes a commit, with a message saying why it changed. Any earlier state can be restored, two states can be compared, and a result can be tied to the exact files that made it. The project’s Python packages are pinned too, in a lockfile (uv.lock, introduced in Section 4.10), so a colleague’s machine builds the same environment, the Python version and packages the code runs with, as yours.
Together these turn the drift problem around. Correct one value in the data, render, and the table, the chart and the sentence that quote it all update together, in every format.


Pause and think


You correct one number in the data. What do you retype in the report?



Answer

Nothing. You fix the data file and render again. If the answer is anything else, some number in the report was typed rather than computed, and that is the bug to fix.








WarningCommon pitfall



Reproducible does not mean correct. A wrong analysis reproduces perfectly: the same wrong number appears in every format, every time. Reproducibility makes errors findable, because anyone can trace a number back to its code and data, but you still have to check results against their sources. Chapter 13 is an extended example of a result that reproduces cleanly and still must not be read the way it first appears.


There is one more subtlety, which matters once projects grow. Rendering every page from scratch can be slow, so Quarto can cache results with a setting called freeze. A cache is only as good as its rule for throwing results away, and Quarto re-executes a frozen page when that page’s source changes, not when a data file it reads changes. Chapter 14 shows how to use the cache safely. This book itself uses one, with a documented way to clear it (Appendix H).

section: 1.5 When Quarto is the wrong tool
text:
1.5 When Quarto is the wrong tool
Quarto earns its keep when the same content is rebuilt, either because the data change or because the content goes to several audiences. It costs you a plain-text workflow, a command line and some setup. That trade is not always worth making:

Collaborators who edit in Word. If the people who revise the document work in a word processor with tracked changes, they can comment on the Word output, but their edits have to be carried back into the source by hand. For documents whose main work is multi-author line editing, a shared word processor may simply fit better.
Designed layouts. Quarto produces structured documents: headings, paragraphs, figures, tables. Typst and CSS can take the look a long way, but a poster or a brand-heavy brochure laid out to the millimetre is easier in a design tool.
Format fidelity at the edges. Each format can only carry what it supports. Pandoc writes good Word and PowerPoint files, but a PowerPoint table cannot hold pictures, for example, so the London guide’s photo table shows each photo’s alt text in its pptx version instead. Check every format you promise to deliver.
One-off documents. A two-paragraph note with no data and no second audience gains little from a build system.







TipIn practice



A useful test: will this document be built a second time? If the data will change, if a second audience will need it in another format, or if someone will ask “where did this number come from?”, the plain-text workflow pays for itself quickly. If none of these is likely, use whatever is fastest.

title: 1  Publishing That Rebuilds Itself
text:
Summary


Reports drift when their outputs are edited by hand; editing one source and letting a program rebuild every output removes the copies.
quarto render executes the code cells, converts the result with Pandoc and, for PDF, typesets it with Typst; the step that stops tells you where to look.
Quarto is conventional software, not AI: the same source and data give the same outputs, so you check the assistant’s work once and anyone can rebuild yours without trusting it.
Reproducible work earns trust, justifies decisions and can be built on. It means one source, computed numbers, one command and versioned files, and it makes errors findable, not absent.
A cache such as freeze re-runs a page when its source changes, not when its data do, so it needs a rule for clearing it.
Quarto pays for documents that will be built again, and is the wrong tool for co-editing in Word, designed layouts and one-off notes.


Quarto, though, renders only what it is given. In this book a coding assistant writes those sources, and its output varies from run to run and can be confidently wrong. How do you ask such a program for work, and how do you check what comes back before anything is published? Chapter 2 answers.

title: 2  Working With a Coding Assistant
text:
2.1 Model plus harness
Simon Willison, a developer, has asked most major new models the same question since 2024: “Generate an SVG of a pelican riding a bicycle” (an SVG is a drawing written as text, so a model writes one as it writes code). Four Claude models, each at three effort levels (how long the model reasons before answering), answered it with 12 drawings, and every one is recognisably a pelican on a bicycle. The dearest cost 13.09 cents, about 93 times as much as the cheapest that was good enough, at 0.14 cents (Figure 2.2).
Choosing between those drawings is the first of many judgements this chapter teaches. A coding assistant is a program that writes and edits files and runs commands at your request: you write the Prompt, it does the typing, and you Check whether the result is right. It can produce in a minute what would take an hour by hand, and it can produce plausible, confident, wrong work just as quickly. How do you get the first kind of work without being fooled by the second?
A coding assistant is two programs working together (Figure 2.1).
The model is a large language model, such as Anthropic’s Claude, OpenAI’s GPT or Google’s Gemini. It runs on the vendor’s servers. It reads text and writes text, and it can reply with a structured request to use a tool: “read this file”, “run this command”.
The harness is the program on your computer that surrounds the model. Claude Code, Codex and Antigravity are harnesses. The harness gives the model its tools (reading and writing files, running commands, searching), carries out the model’s tool requests, asks you before it does anything consequential, and sends the results back to the model. That loop repeats until the model replies with an answer instead of another request.
A short way to remember the split: the model decides, the harness does, you direct and check. It has a practical consequence. Many harnesses can run several models, so the same harness behaves differently with a different model, and the same model behaves differently inside a different harness. When an assistant disappoints you, the cause can be either half, and the fix is different: a stronger model for reasoning that falls short, better rules or permissions for a harness that does the wrong thing.

text:
2.2 Choosing an assistant and a model
This book covers three assistants. Each comes from the same company as its default models:

What “covers” means differs between them. For all three, the install command, the account it needs and how it reads project rules were checked against the vendor’s documentation (dated in Chapter 3 and Section 2.5). The first screens of Claude Code and Codex were captured for the workshop on 2026-11-07; Antigravity’s were not. Other assistants exist; this book does not check them, so it does not list them. Every prompt in the book is written to work in any of the three. A vendor’s own pairing of harness and model is the easiest to set up, but it is not automatically the best fit for a task: the assistant and the model are separate choices.

2.2.1 Pick a model by task, not by rank
Each vendor offers a family of models, from small and cheap to large and capable. They are not simply better and worse versions of one thing. Larger, more recent models usually follow longer instructions, plan multi-step work and recover from their own errors better. Small models are faster and cheaper, and often good enough for short, well-specified edits such as fixing a typo or reformatting a table. Joining two datasets or debugging a failed render rewards the stronger model.
The prompts in this book are short and specific, so a mid-sized model at a moderate effort setting is enough: Claude’s Sonnet on medium effort, or Haiku for small edits, or OpenAI’s Sol on low. For unfamiliar, hard work, the vendors’ own advice starts higher: Anthropic suggests starting with Opus 5.5 for most workloads, and OpenAI with GPT-6 Astra for complex reasoning and coding. Start small, and move up only when a task keeps failing.
Models are priced by the token, a fragment of text of a few characters, with one rate for the text sent to the model (input) and another for the text it writes (output). The prices below are API prices: what a program pays per token when it sends requests to the model directly, through the vendor’s programming interface (the API), rather than through a monthly subscription.

2.3 What a conversation costs
Whether you pay by subscription or by API, use is counted in tokens. Three things raise the cost of a session:

A bigger model costs more per token.
A higher effort setting makes the model write more reasoning tokens per reply.
A longer conversation costs more with every turn, because the model keeps no memory between requests: the harness sends the whole conversation again each time. Everything sent with a request (the conversation so far, the files read, the project’s rules) is the model’s context. Prompt caching makes the repeated part cheaper, not free, and caches expire.

The habits that follow are simple: a mid-sized model at moderate effort, one task per conversation, and a fresh conversation as soon as a task is done. Three commands, typed into the assistant itself rather than run in the terminal (Section 3.4.1), cover them:

/clear matters for quality as well as cost. Old instructions and files read earlier keep steering the model while they remain in the conversation; a fresh conversation drops them. Nothing on disk changes, and the project’s rules file is read again.


Pause and think


One task is finished and an unrelated one starts. Which command first, and what does it keep?



Answer

/clear. The new task needs none of the old conversation, and carrying it along costs tokens on every turn and can mislead the model. Your files stay as they are, and the project’s rules file is read again.

text:
2.4 The root folder is the assistant’s world
An assistant treats the folder you start it in as its root: it reads and edits files there and in the folders below, and runs commands from there. The first time you start one in a new folder, it asks whether you trust it. Claude Code’s prompt, captured on 2026-11-07, warns that “Claude Code’ll be able to read, edit, and execute files here”; Codex asks the same question in a folder that is a Git repository, and says it can read, edit and run files “subject to your permission settings”.
That question deserves a real answer. Trust only a folder you created for the work. Never start an assistant in your home folder, in Documents, or anywhere that holds other people’s projects, private documents or keys (such as ~/.ssh). Project instructions in a trusted folder are read and followed too, which is another reason to trust only your own folders.
Starting in a small project folder has three practical benefits. Paths in prompts stay short (data/attractions.csv), the project’s rules file is found, and a mistake stays inside one folder that you can restore. It is not a guaranteed boundary, though: a command can still name a path outside the folder, so read each command before you approve it.






WarningCommon pitfall



Two assistants writing the same files, or rendering in one folder at once, will collide; Section 6.2 shows the safe split. To work on another project, leave with /exit, change folder, and start the assistant again there.

title: 2  Working With a Coding Assistant
text:
2.5 Rules that persist: AGENTS.md
Everything you tell an assistant in conversation is forgotten when the conversation ends. Rules that must hold in every session go in a file: AGENTS.md, a plain Markdown file at the top of the project folder that the assistant reads at the start of each session. A good one has three parts:

Scope: what the project is, and what it is not.
Rules: what must always hold (“every number comes from a cited file in data/”).
Commands: how to build and check the project.

All three assistants in this book read it (checked 2026-10-30). Codex reads AGENTS.md files before doing any work. Antigravity reads AGENTS.md or GEMINI.md in the project’s folders. Claude Code reads AGENTS.md when there is no CLAUDE.md in the working folder or above it, from version 2.1.277; a CLAUDE.md containing the line @AGENTS.md imports it, so one file can serve all three (Claude Code memory documentation, checked 2026-11-12). The repository behind this book works exactly that way: its CLAUDE.md imports its AGENTS.md.






WarningCommon pitfall



AGENTS.md is context, not enforcement. The assistant reads the rules and usually follows them, but it can still slip. Write rules that are concrete enough to check (“call ALVA counts ‘ALVA member attractions’”), and check them.




Pause and think


Yesterday you told the assistant, in conversation, to say “ALVA member attractions”. Today it writes “top attractions”. Why, and what is the lasting fix?



Answer

The instruction ended with yesterday’s conversation: the model keeps no memory between sessions. Put the rule in AGENTS.md, which is read at the start of every session, and still check for it, because rules are context, not enforcement.


Part II writes the London guide’s rules in Chapter 4, and Part III writes the water analysis’s in Chapter 8.

text:
2.6 How to ask for work
A prompt is the request you type into the assistant. Four habits make prompts reliable:
Be specific. Name the files, the columns, the chart type and the output. “Make a chart” invites guessing; “add a horizontal bar chart of visits_2025 by attraction from data/attractions.csv” does not.
One step at a time. One task per prompt keeps each change small enough to review, and tells you which step broke when one does.
Ask it to run and check. End with a check the assistant can perform: “render it and tell me which file it wrote”, “check that the PDF is one page”. An assistant that verifies its own work catches many of its own mistakes.
Check what changed. You are responsible for the result. Read the changed files (most assistants can show you a diff, the lines added and removed) before moving on.
The prompts in this book were designed with AI assistance and refined to reduce errors, but they are not magic, and assistants vary. When a prompt mentions something you do not understand (a YAML key, a Markdown construct, a Python call), ask before you paste:



Ask your coding assistant

Explain what a Markdown table is and when to use it. Then name the official docs page where I can verify your answer.


Asking for the documentation page matters: it turns the answer into something you can check.

2.6.1 A web chat can draft your prompt
If you know what you want but not how to ask for it, a free web chat (Claude, ChatGPT or Gemini in the browser) can turn a rough idea into a prompt. Describe the goal in plain words, name your tools, and ask for a prompt of one to four lines, with one task, concrete file names and a check (Figure 2.3). The chat cannot see your files, so it guesses; the assistant can see them, so it checks. Read the drafted prompt before you paste it, and fix any file name that does not match your folder.






Figure 2.3: A web chat drafts a prompt, you read it, and the coding assistant runs it. An illustration drawn for the workshop, not a recording: real replies vary.









WarningCommon pitfall



Paste only what you would be happy to publish. Web chats and assistants send your text to the vendor: no passwords, keys, unpublished data or personal information.

Every hands-on step in this book uses the same three-part box. Here is a simpler version of the first one you will meet in Part II:

Ask your coding assistant holds the exact prompt to paste into the assistant (in the HTML edition, with a copy button). Expect it to run lists what the assistant will probably do, so you recognise it when it asks for approval; you do not type these yourself. You do lists the few things only you can do: start the assistant, sign in to accounts, approve commands, run a live preview, open results. The assistant occupies the terminal tab it runs in, so commands in a You do box go in a second terminal tab opened in the same folder (Section 3.4.1).
Together the boxes are one turn of the loop in the book’s title. Ask your coding assistant is the Prompt. Expect it to run and You do are where you Check, recognising each command before you approve it and opening the result yourself. The render is the Publish. Each exercise closes the loop with You’re done when: the check, stated so that you can see whether it passed.






WarningCommon pitfall



Approving a command without reading it. Most commands in this book run a tool the prompt named (quarto, uv, git, gh) on files in the project folder. Stop and ask the assistant what a command does before you approve one that deletes files (rm), runs as the administrator (sudo), or touches a folder outside the project that the prompt did not name.


The prompts are examples, not transcripts. Assistants vary from version to version and run to run, so the files they write will differ in detail from the ones shown. What should not vary is the result you check. Figure 2.4 shows what a session looks like.

text:
2.8 Using AI in research: say it, own it
If your work is research, using an assistant raises obligations beyond getting the code right. Journals and funders differ in detail, so read your venue’s own policy, but the International Committee of Medical Journal Editors (ICMJE), whose recommendations many journals follow, states a common core (checked 2026-11-12):

An AI tool is never an author. Chatbots and other AI-assisted tools “should not be listed as authors because they cannot be responsible for the accuracy, integrity, and originality of the work”.
You are responsible for what it produced. Humans are responsible for any submitted material that used AI-assisted technologies, and should review and edit AI output, which “can be incorrect, incomplete, or biased”. That includes references: AI-generated material is not an acceptable primary source.
Disclose the use. Authors describe their use of AI-assisted technologies at submission, in the cover letter and in the appropriate section of the work.

Two further rules follow from ordinary research ethics rather than from any one policy. Keep unpublished manuscripts, participant data and other confidential material out of public AI tools. And never let a tool generate or alter primary data or images: presenting generated data as observed is fabrication.
A useful disclosure names the tool and version, the tasks it performed and the checks you made. The statement for this book, on its copyright page, is written that way. Where it goes depends on the use: code and analysis belong in the Methods, with enough detail to reproduce them, which in a Quarto project means the code itself and the project’s AGENTS.md.


Pause and think


Which needs a statement: fixing a typo, or computing a table?



Answer

Computing a table is analysis: describe it in the Methods, in enough detail to reproduce. Venues differ on whether language editing needs a statement; ICMJE’s recommendations make no exception for it, so when in doubt, disclose.

Summary


The model decides, the harness does, and you direct and check; when an assistant disappoints, either half can be the cause.
Choose a model by the task, not by rank: as the pelicans showed, a cheaper model at medium effort is often enough for a small, well-specified step.
Cost grows with model size, effort and conversation length, because the whole conversation is sent again each turn, so start a fresh conversation for each unrelated task.

Rules that must last go in AGENTS.md, which is context, not enforcement, so write them concretely enough to check.
Good prompts are specific, ask for one step and end in a check; in research the assistant is never an author, and its use is disclosed.


All of this assumes a computer on which an assistant, Quarto and Python are installed and working together. Is yours? Chapter 3 gets it there in six checked steps.

3.1 Before you start
This chapter ends with a number: 42, printed in a web page and a PDF that your own computer built. Getting it there proves that the assistant, Python, Quarto and Typst work together. That is all Parts II and III need, because everything in them happens on your machine: the assistant writes files in your folders, Quarto renders them there, and you open the results in your own browser and word processor. It takes six steps, and each ends with a check you can see, so you always know whether a step worked before you move on.
Do the setup somewhere calm, with a good connection, and allow about an hour. Mac and Linux readers can follow this chapter straight through. Windows readers first install Ubuntu, a version of Linux, inside Windows with WSL, the Windows Subsystem for Linux; Appendix A walks through that one step at a time, and from then on they follow this chapter inside Ubuntu.
A stable, fast connection. Almost every step downloads something: on Windows the Ubuntu image (several hundred megabytes), then Quarto, uv (which manages Python for each project) and Python packages, the assistant itself and the example projects with their data. The assistant also sends every request to its model over the internet, so a weak connection shows up as long pauses, timeouts and half-finished installs, which are easy to mistake for your own errors. Use a wired connection or strong Wi-Fi, avoid VPNs where you can, and expect company networks with a proxy to block some downloads.
Two accounts. A free GitHub account, used to publish in Parts II and III, and an account with access to one coding assistant. Claude Code needs a Pro, Max, Team, Enterprise or Console account; Codex a ChatGPT sign-in or an API key (for pay-per-use billing, Section 2.2); Antigravity a Google account (checked 2026-11-03). Sign-up and email verification can take hours, so do them first.
A plan for when a step fails. Errors during setup are normal: each step depends on your system, your network and that week’s versions, so an error does not mean you have failed. It tells you what to fix:

❯ Try "write a test for <filepath>"
────────────────────────────────────────────────────







ImportantTry it



Install one assistant, start it in ~/setup, sign in and trust the folder.

You’re done when the assistant answers when you type hello. Then type /exit.




3.4.1 Two places to type
Now that an assistant is installed, there are two places to type, and mixing them up costs beginners more time than anything else.
ana@laptop:~/setup$ pwd                  <- the terminal: commands
❯ Which tools are missing?                <- the assistant: requests in plain language
The assistant takes over the terminal tab it runs in: what you type there goes to the assistant, not to the shell, the program behind the terminal that runs your commands, until you leave with /exit. Commands in this book’s You do boxes, such as quarto preview, go in the terminal; prompts in Ask your coding assistant boxes go to the assistant. When the assistant is busy and you need the terminal, open a second tab, as after the install.
Typing in the wrong place is usually harmless: a prompt typed at $ gives command not found, and a command typed into the assistant is read as a request. Look at the line you are on and try again.


Pause and think


The assistant is running and the book says to type gh auth login, the GitHub sign-in of Step 5. Where do you type it?



Answer

In a second terminal tab: gh auth login is an interactive sign-in that needs you, and the assistant is using the first tab. Leaving the assistant with /exit also works, but ends the conversation.

3.5 Step 4: Let the assistant install the tools
The remaining tools are Quarto itself, uv, Git and the GitHub command-line tool gh. Each has its own official install method for each system, which is exactly the kind of detail an assistant handles well. Start it again in the setup folder (with codex or agy in place of claude if that is your assistant, here and in the next steps):



You do

mkdir -p ~/setup && cd ~/setup && claude    # or: codex, or: agy



Ask your coding assistant

Check which of `git`, `curl`, `uv`, `quarto` (1.10 or newer) and the GitHub CLI `gh` are missing on this computer. Install only those, using each tool's official method for my system. Never run `sudo`, or an installer that asks for a password, yourself: print each such command alone in a code block, using full paths, then wait until I say done. Then print every version.



Expect it to run

installs uv with its official installer · Quarto from its release page (or Homebrew on a Mac) · gh from GitHub’s own package source · prints versions


Before each command it wants to run, the assistant stops and asks, as in Figure 2.4: read the command (the pitfall in Section 2.7 says what to look for), then approve it.
The prompt is written around one limitation: an assistant cannot type your password. So it asks the assistant to hand back any command that needs one, with full paths, because the second tab you paste it into starts in your home folder. Copy the command (Ctrl+Shift+C, or Command-C on a Mac), paste it in a second tab, type your password when sudo asks (it stays invisible), and then type done in the assistant’s tab. On a Mac, the password is your login password.






NoteWhy this works



Quarto has no Ubuntu package in the standard repositories, and Ubuntu’s own gh package is discouraged by GitHub, so a generic apt install would get one tool wrong and the other missing. The prompt’s “each tool’s official method” sends the assistant to the right source for each (Quarto’s download page and GitHub’s install instructions for Linux, checked 2026-10-30).




Pause and think


The assistant has installed uv. In a terminal tab you opened before that, you type uv --version, and the terminal answers command not found. Did the install fail?



Answer

Probably not. uv’s installer puts it in ~/.local/bin, which a terminal adds to its PATH only when it starts, so a tab opened earlier cannot find it. Open a new tab and try again; only if it fails there is the install at fault.








ImportantTry it



Paste the prompt, approve the commands you have read, and run any sudo command it hands you in a second tab.

You’re done when it prints a version for all five tools. Then type /exit: uv and Quarto are only found by a terminal started after they were installed.

3.6 Step 5: Run the setup check
Open a new tab and start the assistant again, so that it sees the newly installed tools:



You do

cd ~/setup && claude    # or: codex, or: agy



Ask your coding assistant

Print the versions of `quarto` (1.10 or newer), `uv`, `gh` and this assistant, and run `quarto check` (no Jupyter or LaTeX yet is fine: count it as OK). If `git config --global user.name` or `user.email` is unset, ask me for my name and my GitHub email, then set them. Clone https://github.com/project-delphi/quarto-workshop.git to `~/quarto-workshop` (if it exists, `git pull` only when its working tree is clean) and list its `checkpoints/`. Run `gh auth status`. Run every check even if one fails, then report each as OK or not.


Three parts of this check deserve a word.
quarto check reports Quarto’s own components, including Pandoc and Typst. Its Python and Jupyter lines may say they are missing, and that is fine: each project in this book gets its own Python environment from uv, so there is nothing to install for Python now. No LaTeX is needed either, because PDFs are made with the Typst engine bundled in Quarto.
A fresh Git has no identity, and git commit refuses to run without one. The prompt makes the assistant ask you for your name and email, so you type your own; check that what it set is yours, not a placeholder.
To clone is to copy a repository, with its history, to your computer: here the workshop’s, into ~/quarto-workshop. It holds the finished examples, the water dataset and the checkpoints: snapshots of each project at the end of each hands-on block, which you will use to catch up if you fall behind.



You do

if gh is not “Logged in”: in a second tab, gh auth login → GitHub.com → HTTPS → Yes → log in with a web browser; copy the one-time code to github.com/login/device; then ask the assistant to check gh again








ImportantTry it



Run the setup check.

You’re done when the assistant reports every check as OK, including gh “Logged in”.

text:
3.7 Step 6: The test run
The setup check proves the tools are installed. The test run proves they work together: the assistant can write a file and run commands you approve, uv can build a project environment, Quarto can run Python through it, and Typst can write a PDF.



You do

mkdir -p ~/quarto-test && cd ~/quarto-test
claude          # or: codex, or: agy



Ask your coding assistant

Run `uv init --bare` and `uv add ipykernel nbclient nbformat pyyaml`. Create hello.qmd (html and typst formats): a Python cell computing `6 * 7` and an inline-code sentence showing it. Render it with `uv run quarto render hello.qmd`; check hello.html and hello.pdf both say 42.



Expect it to run

uv init --bare · uv add … · writes hello.qmd · uv run quarto render hello.qmd → hello.html, hello.pdf



You do

/exit, then open the folder: open . (Mac), xdg-open . (Linux) or explorer.exe . (WSL), and open both files


The test run uses things the next chapters explain, YAML settings, a code cell and inline code, on purpose: it is a black-box check that the tools work together, not a lesson. If you are curious, hello.qmd is the file shown in Section 1.2.






WarningCommon pitfall



Every render prints a line such as [IPKernelApp] WARNING | Kernel is running over TCP without encryption. It is harmless: Quarto talks to the Python kernel, the running Python process that executes the cells, over a local connection on your own computer, and in every dry run the warning came with a successful render and changed nothing in the output.








ImportantTry it



Run the test run and open both outputs.

You’re done when hello.html and hello.pdf both say 42. The folder is disposable: delete ~/quarto-test afterwards. If a file is missing or says something else, see the Python and Jupyter table in Appendix D.

The test run was a black box: a file you did not write, settings you have not met, code you have not read. Part II opens it. title: Part II: One Guide, Many Audiences
text:
London’s tourism office has one set of facts and many readers. Visitors want a web page they can open on a phone. Managers want the numbers at a glance, partners a brief they can forward, and people who walk in off the street something to take away. The office needs every one of those versions to say the same thing, and to go on saying it when the visitor counts are revised.
In this part you play the office’s role. You write the guide once, from cited data, and let Quarto make every version from that one source:

4  Markdown, Rendering and Project Rules turns an empty folder into a web page that changes as you watch, with written rules that hold the assistant to cited facts.
5  Documents That Compute makes the guide compute: the numbers in its sentences and its chart come from the data, in three formats at once.
6  One Guide, Five Audiences serves managers, partners and walk-ins in one step, with your assistant directing three sub-agents side by side.
7  Publishing and Proving the Rebuild puts the guide on the web, then changes one number and asks you to explain everything that changed with it.

The exercises at the end of the part test whether you can do it without the prompts.



Where we are: Part II.

title: 4  Markdown, Rendering and Project Rules
text:
4.1 Markdown at a glance
The tourism office wants a visitor guide it can stand behind: a page anyone can open on a phone, every fact traced to a source, rebuilt rather than retyped when the facts change. Figure 4.1 is where Part II ends: the guide on its own website, with links to the same content in Word, PDF, PowerPoint, e-book and slide formats.
It starts as an empty folder and one plain-text file in Markdown, a way of writing structured text with a few punctuation marks. The assistant writes most of it, but Markdown is what you check: the layer you review, compare between versions and fix by hand when a sentence is wrong.
More is new here than in any other chapter: the assistant, the rules, the preview and the environment. Work through it in order: read a section, paste its prompt and look at the result before moving on; each Try it box says what you should see by then. When a step goes wrong, nothing is lost: one line pasted into the assistant restores the chapter’s finished state (Section 4.11).
Markdown is plain text in which a few symbols mean formatting. A # at the start of a line makes a heading; two stars on each side of a word make it bold. You type the symbols, and when Quarto renders the file, turning it into a page, it puts the formatting in their place. A Markdown file is an ordinary text file whose name ends in .md: any plain-text editor opens it, and it reads well even before it is rendered.
This section shows the marks one at a time, before the first prompt; the sections after it use each of them in the guide. Each animation pairs what you type, on the left, with what you get, on the right. The right-hand side is not drawn: each step on the left was saved in a file and rendered by Quarto 1.10.20, and the right shows that page, enlarged. Each animation opens on its finished pair, then types the source from the beginning.
Two things make Markdown safe to learn by trying:
crumbs: Part II: One Guide, Many Audiences
4  Markdown, Rendering and Project Rules

title: 4  Markdown, Rendering and Project Rules
text:
Nothing breaks. A mark that is mistyped, or opened and never closed, shows on the page as an ordinary character. The page still renders, the stray symbol is easy to spot, and you fix it by editing the text.
Trying costs nothing. Type a few lines into a new file named try.md, then run quarto preview try.md in the terminal, in that file’s folder (Section 4.1.6). The page opens in your browser and changes every time you save the file; Ctrl+C in the terminal stops it.


4.1.1 Headings, paragraphs and emphasis
A line that starts with # and a space is a heading, the title of a part of the page. One # gives the largest heading, for the page’s title. Each extra # makes a heading one level smaller (Figure 4.2), down to six.






Figure 4.2: Headings: one # for the largest, then ## and ### for each level down. The page is shown at a laptop’s width, where the three sizes differ most.



Ordinary text needs no mark. Lines that follow one another join into one paragraph, wherever you break them, and a blank line, a line with nothing on it, starts a new paragraph (Figure 4.3). So you can break a long sentence over several lines of the file without changing the page.






Figure 4.3: Paragraphs: lines next to each other join into one paragraph, and a blank line starts the next.



Stars round words emphasise them: two on each side for bold, one on each side for italic. Two tildes (~) on each side strike text through, for something no longer true. These marks come in pairs. Until the closing pair is typed, the opening one shows as typed, as at the start of Figure 4.4.






Figure 4.4: Emphasis: **bold**, *italic* and ~~struck through~~. Until its closing ** is typed, the opening pair shows as two stars.





4.1.2 Lists, quotations and lines
A line that starts with - and a space is an item in a bulleted list. A number and a full stop, such as 1., then a space, start an item in a numbered list (Figure 4.5). Leave a blank line above a list: without one, its items run on as part of the paragraph before it.






Figure 4.5: Lists: - and a space for a bulleted item, 1. and a space for a numbered one, with a blank line between the two lists.



A > at the start of a line makes a block quote: a quotation, set off from the text beside a bar (Figure 4.6). Start each of its lines with >.






Figure 4.6: A block quote: > at the start of each line sets the lines off as a quotation.



Three dashes on a line of their own, with a blank line above and below, draw a horizontal rule: a line across the page that separates two parts of it (Figure 4.7).






Figure 4.7: A horizontal rule: --- on a line of its own, between blank lines.





4.1.3 Links and pictures
A link has two parts: the words to click, in square brackets, then the address they open, in round brackets, with no space between the two (Figure 4.8). Square brackets on their own show as typed. An address is often too long for one row of the screen, so the editor wraps it, showing the rest on the next row, as on the left of Figure 4.8. It is still one line, typed without pressing Enter.






Figure 4.8: A link: the words in square brackets, then the address in round brackets. With the square brackets alone, the words show as typed.



A picture is written like a link with a ! in front: its caption in square brackets, then its file in round brackets (Figure 4.9). Here the file, hall.jpg, is in the same folder as the Markdown file. Section 4.7 adds what a published picture also needs: a size, and alt text, a description for readers who cannot see it.






Figure 4.9: A picture: !, the caption in square brackets, the file in round brackets. Photo of the Natural History Museum’s Central Hall: Julian Herzog, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.



A picture can be a link too. Put the whole picture where a link’s words go, inside its square brackets: [![caption](file)](address) (Figure 4.10). The page looks the same, but a click on the photo opens the address, here the museum’s own page for visitors.






Figure 4.10: A picture that is a link: the picture takes the place of a link’s words. The page looks the same, and a click on the photo opens the museum’s page. Photo: Julian Herzog, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.





4.1.4 All the marks together
Table 4.1 and Table 4.2 gather the marks this book uses, those above and a few more, each with the section where the guide first needs it. Come back to them as you write.



Table 4.1: Markdown for text and lists.









You type
You get




# Visit London
a heading; ## is the next level down (Section 4.3)

italic, bold (Section 4.3)

an item with an empty box; [x] ticks it






To break a line without starting a new paragraph, end it with \. Two spaces at the end work too, but “the backslash is easier to see, and editors that strip trailing whitespace on save won’t remove it” (Quarto, Markdown Basics).



Table 4.2: Markdown for links, pictures and blocks.

You get

*free*, stars and all: \ before a mark keeps it as typed






Here is every one of those marks in one file, toy.md, a short London note with no settings and no code:

# A day in London

Start at the **British Museum**,
where entry is *free*.\
Get there by:

- Tube
- Bus
- ~~Car~~

> Tip: book a free timed ticket.

## Two sights

1. British Museum
2. Tower of London

| Sight           | Price |
|-----------------|-------|
| British Museum  | Free  |
| Tower of London | Paid  |

---

![Big Ben](big-ben.jpg){width=15%
fig-alt="Big Ben's clock tower."}

Photo: John Dillenbeck, CC0.
Plan a route with
[TfL](https://tfl.gov.uk/).
Built with `quarto render`.
Stars kept, not italic: \*free\*

- [x] Contactless card
- [ ] Umbrella

```text
In a fence, **marks** stay put.
```

quarto render toy.md turns it into toy.html, Figure 4.11. Compare the two line by line: the lines of each paragraph have joined, except where a \ broke one; “Car” is struck through; the escaped stars round “free” and the stars inside the fence have stayed stars.






Figure 4.11: What quarto render toy.md makes of the file, at a phone’s width: a screenshot of toy.html as Quarto 1.10.20 renders it. Photo of Big Ben: John Dillenbeck, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.





Pause and think


A line of text, and straight under it, with no blank line between, a line of three dashes. Does the page show a horizontal rule?



Answer

No: the line of text becomes a level-2 heading. A line underlined with dashes is another way of writing one, in GFM and in Pandoc’s Markdown alike, which is why the rule in Table 4.2 needs a blank line above it.




4.1.5 GitHub’s Markdown and Quarto’s
Markdown comes in dialects. GitHub Flavored Markdown (GFM) is the one GitHub uses for what people write there, such as README files and issues. It is “a strict superset of CommonMark”, a precise specification of Markdown, with five extensions: tables, task lists, strikethrough, automatic links and a ban on some raw HTML (GFM specification, version 0.29-gfm, checked 2026-11-12).
Quarto “is based on Pandoc and uses its variation of markdown as its underlying document syntax” (Quarto, Markdown Basics, checked 2026-11-12). Pandoc’s Markdown reads the same core marks as GFM, takes its task lists from it, and adds more: attributes in braces, footnotes, definition lists, citations and mathematics among them (Pandoc User’s Guide, checked 2026-11-12). Three differences catch people who learnt Markdown on GitHub:

A list needs a blank line above it; without one, it runs on as part of the paragraph.
Strikethrough needs two tildes, ~~Car~~, because a single pair, ~2~, makes a subscript.
An image’s text in square brackets is its caption in Quarto, where GitHub uses it as alt text; Quarto’s alt text goes in fig-alt (Section 4.7).



4.1.6 Two commands: render and preview
Quarto turns a file into a page with either of two commands, typed in the terminal in the file’s folder (quarto render --help and quarto preview --help, Quarto 1.10.20, checked 2026-11-12):

quarto render toy.md

writes the output once, here toy.html, and stops. --to docx picks another format. Use it to make a finished file, the one you send or publish.

quarto preview toy.md

renders the file, serves the page on a local address and renders it again each time the file is saved; Ctrl+C stops it. Use it while you write, in a terminal tab of its own.


A plain .md file needs no settings to render, as toy.md shows. Section 4.4 runs both commands on the guide.

4.2 A folder for the guide
The guide gets its own folder in your home folder, beside the quarto-workshop repository (a project folder with its Git history) that you cloned during setup (Section 3.6), so that its checkpoints are always at ../quarto-workshop/checkpoints/. By the end of the chapter your home folder, ~, looks like this:
~
├── quarto-workshop/
└── london-guide/
    ├── AGENTS.md
    ├── london.md
    ├── london.html
    ├── data/
    ├── images/
    ├── pyproject.toml
    ├── uv.lock
    └── .venv/

AGENTS.md: the rules the assistant reads first.
london.md: the guide’s source, the file you check; london.html is rendered from it.
data/ and images/: cited facts and credited photos, copied in and never edited.
pyproject.toml, uv.lock and .venv/: the packages, their exact versions and the installed environment.

Make the folder and start the assistant in it:



You do

cd ~
mkdir -p london-guide
cd london-guide
claude    # or: codex, or: agy


Claude Code first asks whether you trust the new folder (Section 3.4): you made it for this work, so say yes. Later prompts copy files from ../quarto-workshop/, which is outside the project folder, so the assistant asks your permission the first time it reads there. Approve it, or start Claude Code with claude --add-dir ../quarto-workshop to allow it up front (Codex has the same option, --add-dir).

4.4 Watch it become a web page



Ask your coding assistant

Render london.md with quarto render and tell me which file it wrote.



Expect it to run

quarto render london.md → london.html



You do

in a second terminal tab:
cd ~/london-guide

open the address it prints · Ctrl+C stops it


The render writes london.html once. The preview (Section 4.1) renders it again every time london.md is saved, including when the assistant saves it, so the page in your browser follows each change (Figure 4.12). It prints a line such as Browse at http://localhost:4200/ (the number varies) and usually opens that page in your browser; if it does not, open the address yourself.






Figure 4.12: A live preview: each time london.md is saved (left), quarto preview renders it again and the page reloads (right). A real recording of quarto preview with the edits this chapter makes.



Keep the preview running from now on. It is the fastest way to check what each prompt did.

A preview and a render of the same file at the same moment collide: both write temporary files with the same names, and one fails with an error such as readfile 'london.quarto_ipynb'. While a preview is running, let it do the rendering. Before the assistant renders several formats at once (Section 5.5), stop the preview with Ctrl+C, and restart it afterwards.

title: 4  Markdown, Rendering and Project Rules
text:
4.5 Rules for the guide
Section 2.5 introduced AGENTS.md, the file of rules an assistant reads at the start of every session. The guide needs one now, before any data or photos arrive, because every later prompt relies on it:



Ask your coding assistant

Create AGENTS.md for this project. Scope: a London visitor guide for the tourism office, written once and reused for every audience. Rules: every number comes from a cited file in data/, photos are openly licensed, credited and show no people, never invent facts, keep data/ and images/ unchanged, and call ALVA counts "ALVA member attractions". Show me the file.



Expect it to run

writes AGENTS.md: a scope and a list of rules



You do

approve · read it: does it say what you meant?


Each rule is there for a reason the project will meet. Every number comes from a cited file: the guide quotes visitor counts, and an assistant asked for a number it does not have may produce a plausible one; a rule that every figure is computed from a file with a source removes that temptation, and gives you something to check. Openly licensed photos with no people: a published guide needs images it may reuse, and pictures of identifiable people raise consent questions it does not need. Keep data/ and images/ unchanged: the inputs are evidence, and edits belong in the analysis, not in the evidence. “ALVA member attractions”: the counts come from the Association of Leading Visitor Attractions, which lists only its members, so “London’s most visited attractions” would overclaim.
The finished project’s version reads, in part:
## Rules

- Every number comes from a cited file in `data/`: each row carries `source`, `url` and
  `retrieved`. Never estimate or invent a figure or a fact.
- ALVA counts only its member sites: write "ALVA member attractions".
- Photos are openly licensed, credited from `images/ATTRIBUTION.md`, and show no people.
- Keep `data/` and `images/` unchanged.
Read what the assistant wrote and edit it yourself if the wording is off. It is your project’s contract with the assistant, and the rules work best when they are concrete enough to check. Any plain-text editor will do, or the terminal’s own: in a new tab, cd ~/london-guide, then nano AGENTS.md opens the file; Ctrl+O and Enter save it, and Ctrl+X leaves (Appendix B).

text:
4.10 An environment for the code to come
A Python environment is a folder holding one version of Python and the packages a project uses, kept apart from every other project’s. Packages are the add-on libraries that Python code imports, such as pandas for tables or matplotlib for charts. The next chapter runs Python, and code never runs in a vacuum: what it does depends on the Python version and on the exact version of each package.
Getting all of that to agree used to be a lesson of its own: install conda or a system Python, sometimes a compiler, fix the PATH (the list of folders where the terminal looks for programs), register a Jupyter kernel, then debug it on every laptop. uv now does it in one step, for one project at a time. It fetches the Python version a project needs, and its lockfile, uv.lock, records the exact version of every package: it “captures the packages that would be installed across all possible Python markers such as operating system, architecture, and Python version” (uv documentation, checked 2026-10-31), so one file reproduces the same environment on every Mac, Windows and Linux machine. Other languages pair a project file with a lockfile in the same way: R’s renv.lock, JavaScript’s package-lock.json, Rust’s Cargo.lock.






NoteWhy this works



Why does the lockfile need to know the computer? Many scientific packages contain compiled C, C++ or Fortran, built separately for each operating system and processor (Intel and AMD x86_64, or Apple and other ARM arm64). Each package file’s platform tag, such as macosx_11_0_arm64, names the system it fits (Python Packaging Authority, checked 2026-10-31), so the lockfile lists the right file for every system.





Ask your coding assistant

Give this folder its own Python environment with `uv`: run `uv init --bare`, then `uv add ipykernel nbclient nbformat pyyaml pandas matplotlib plotly`. From now on run `quarto` and `python` through `uv run`, and add that rule to AGENTS.md. Show me the Python line of `uv run quarto check jupyter`.



Expect it to run

writes pyproject.toml (the packages), uv.lock (their exact versions) and .venv/ (the installed environment) · adds a rule to AGENTS.md








Figure 4.14: Giving the guide its own environment: uv init --bare, uv add with the guide’s packages, and Quarto finding the project’s own Python. A real recording with a demo account; the 40-second first render of the engine check is cut.



The four packages ipykernel, nbclient, nbformat and pyyaml are what Quarto needs to run Python cells; pandas, matplotlib and plotly are what the guide’s code will use. The larger jupyter package, with its notebook applications, is not needed.1
1 Measured in a dry run on 2026-10-30, on one fast connection, a cold install of Part III’s larger package set took 8 seconds with uv and 31 seconds with pip plus jupyter. That compares the old route with the new one, not the two installers like for like, since the pip run also installed jupyter.





NoteWhy this works



Why uv run in front of every command? Quarto refuses to run Python next to a .venv folder that is not activated (“There is an unactivated Python environment in .venv”). uv run activates the project’s environment for that one command, and first brings .venv up to date with uv.lock. So a copied project, or a checkpoint, rebuilds its own environment on its first uv run, and the rule in AGENTS.md keeps the assistant using it after a restart.

Which file tells you the exact version of pandas the guide uses: pyproject.toml or uv.lock?



Answer

uv.lock. pyproject.toml lists the packages the project asked for, each with only a lowest acceptable version (pandas>=…); uv.lock records the one version installed, for every system. That is the file that makes a colleague’s uv run build the same environment as yours.

5.1 The anatomy of a .qmd file
In 2024, by ALVA’s count, the most visited of the guide’s five sights was the British Museum, with 6,479,952 visits; in 2025, the Natural History Museum, with 7,116,929. A guide that said, in typed words, that the British Museum is the most visited of the five went on saying it after ALVA published its 2025 table, in every copy, until someone noticed.
This chapter makes the guide compute instead. Code reads the data at every render, so a new table corrects every sentence, the chart drawn from it and the Word and PDF versions at once, without a single number copied by hand. That is the workflow’s central promise, and the rest of the book builds on it.
A Markdown file can only say what you typed into it. A Quarto document, a .qmd file, can also compute what it says, so before the guide becomes one, here are the parts of one. Ask your coding assistant

The assistant writes a code cell (Section 5.1) and a sentence that uses its results:
```{python}
import pandas as pd
attractions = pd.read_csv("data/attractions.csv")
top = attractions.loc[attractions["visits_2025"].idxmax()]
top_name = top["attraction"]
top_visits = f"{top['visits_2025']:,}"

```

Most visited in 2025: the `{python} top_name`, with `{python} top_visits` visits.
London's ten most visited ALVA member attractions drew `{python} total_visits` visits.
You do not need to write Python to check it, but you should be able to read it. The cell does four things:

import pandas as pd loads pandas, the package for tables, under the short name pd.
pd.read_csv(...) reads the CSV file into a table, attractions, one row per attraction.
attractions["visits_2025"].idxmax() finds the row with the most visits in 2025, and .loc[…] takes that row, so top["attraction"] is its name.
.sum() adds up the column, and f"{…:,}" writes a number as text with a comma between the thousands, ready for a sentence.

When the document renders, the cell runs and its variables are kept, so each piece of inline code, `{python} name`, is replaced by the value of name. Rendered in this book from the same data file, the sentence reads:

Most visited in 2025: the Natural History Museum (South Kensington), with 7,116,929 visits. London’s ten most visited ALVA member attractions drew 39,692,434 visits.

Quarto 1.4 introduced this inline syntax, one for every engine, Python included; R users already wrote inline code with knitr’s `r x`, a syntax Quarto still supports (Quarto 1.4 release notes, checked 2026-11-12).

If attractions.csv changes, which values in those two sentences update?

text:
5.7 What a render does, and why two renders collide
Figure 1.2 in Section 1.2 showed the three steps of a render. With code in the document, the first step is worth looking at more closely, because it explains the commonest failure of this chapter.
To run the cells, Quarto writes the document out as a temporary Jupyter notebook, named after the file (london.quarto_ipynb), starts a Python kernel (a running Python process) from the project’s environment, sends it each cell in order, and collects the results. Two consequences follow. The cells share one Python session, top to bottom, so a later cell can use a variable from an earlier one, and the order of cells matters. And two renders of the same file at the same moment write the same temporary files, which is why a render started while a preview is re-rendering fails with readfile 'london.quarto_ipynb'.
Every render runs every cell again. That is Quarto’s default (freeze: false), and this book’s projects keep it deliberately, so outputs always match the data. It also means a slow cell slows every render; Chapter 14 returns to the trade-off and to freeze: auto, which caches results and needs a rule for when to throw them away.
Each render also prints the harmless IPKernelApp warning described in Section 3.7.


Pause and think


A later cell uses attractions, which an earlier cell creates. You move the later cell above the earlier one. What happens at the next render?



Answer

It fails with a NameError: the cells run top to bottom in one Python session, so attractions does not exist yet when the moved cell runs.

6.1 Content once, format per audience
Correct one fact, then count the documents that repeat it. Written by hand, a dashboard, a partner brief and a printed flyer each hold their own copy of the same facts, and every copy has to be found and fixed. The one that is missed is the one that disagrees in public.
This chapter writes all three in one step: a dashboard for managers, a Word brief and its covering email for partners, and a flyer for walk-ins. The dashboard and the brief read the same data file, so a corrected count reaches both; the flyer copies its facts from data/sights.csv, a choice Section 7.5 returns to. None of the three needs another to exist, which makes them the first job in this book worth splitting across several assistants at once, and the first chance to ask when that is worth what it costs.
Correct is not enough. A document does its job only when its reader engages with it, and each reader meets it differently: a manager scans a dashboard in seconds, a partner forwards a brief, a passer-by gives a flyer a glance. So each format here is chosen for how its reader will use it, and the test for every output is the same: would that reader read it, and act on it?
Each audience gets the format that suits it, and each format is a setting. This chapter makes the first three outputs in Table 6.1 and the optional advert; Chapter 7 makes the website.
A dashboard is a page of charts and key numbers arranged in a grid. In a .qmd file with format: dashboard, a level-1 heading starts a page, a level-2 heading starts a row, and each cell’s output becomes a card in that row (Quarto dashboards documentation, checked 2026-10-31). The guide’s dashboard has two pages; its outline, without the code, is:
# Attractions and # Churches start the two pages, and {height=25%} gives the first row a quarter of the page’s height. That row holds the value boxes, each showing one key number with a label and an icon; the next row holds the charts, one card per cell. A value box is written as a div: a block of Markdown between two lines of three colons, whose class in braces, .valuebox, tells Quarto what to make of it. Quarto’s other special blocks, such as callouts, use the same syntax.
It also needs a second data file. data/visits.csv holds the yearly visits to the five sights from 2015 to 2025, from ALVA’s annual tables. Two notes travel with it, from the data’s README. The years 2020 and 2021 are pandemic years, not comparable with the others. And from 2024 the Natural History Museum’s count includes its reopened gardens, so for that museum 2024 and 2025 are not like-for-like with earlier years. data/churches.csv lists the ten cathedrals and churches on Visit London’s own list, an editorial choice with no visitor numbers.
A Word brief turns Markdown headings into Word’s heading styles, so the partner’s copy has a navigable outline and working links. Its covering email is not rendered at all: it is a plain Markdown file whose message sits in a text block, to be copied into an email client, with the brief attached. The email deliberately quotes no visitor numbers. The numbers stay in the brief, where they are computed and cited, as the project’s rules require.
A flyer is a one-page Typst PDF on A5 paper. papersize accepts any of Typst’s paper names (a5, a4, us-letter and so on), and margin sets the margins (Quarto’s Typst documentation, checked 2026-10-30).

6.2 Sub-agents: one lead, many hands
The three outputs are independent: none needs another to exist. That makes them a candidate for sub-agents, separate assistant sessions that your assistant starts for one task each (Figure 6.3). Each sub-agent has its own context, does its task and reports back; your assistant, the lead, waits for all of them and then checks the results.






Figure 6.3: One lead, three sub-agents. Each writes only its own files and renders nothing; the lead renders the files one at a time.



The gain is time: three independent tasks take about as long as the slowest of them. The cost is tokens, because each sub-agent does its own reading, reasoning and tool calls. The three assistants differ in how they offer it (all checked 2026-10-31). Claude Code starts sub-agents in parallel when a prompt asks for them. Codex enables sub-agents by default and starts them when asked, and its documentation warns both that parallel edits “can create conflicts” and that sub-agent runs use more tokens. Antigravity’s command-line agent can delegate to parallel sub-agents, but its documentation does not say a prompt can require it, so it may do the tasks itself.
Two rules make parallel work safe, and the prompt below states both. Each sub-agent writes only its own files and renders nothing, so no two of them touch the same file. The lead renders the files one at a time, because two Quarto renders, or two environment updates by uv run, in the same folder can collide. Sub-agents read AGENTS.md too, so the project’s rules still apply to their work.






TipIn practice



Use sub-agents when tasks are independent, substantial and write different files. Do not use them for tasks where one needs another’s result, for several edits to the same file, or for small tasks where the overhead of starting and briefing a sub-agent outweighs the work. A prompt that might run without sub-agents should say what to do then: the prompt below ends its first sentence with “none? do the items in turn”.




Pause and think


The office also wants the guide in French and Spanish, each a new file made from london.qmd. Is that a job for sub-agents?



Answer

Yes: the two translations are independent, substantial and write different files (say london-fr.qmd and london-es.qmd), and the lead renders them one at a time. If both first needed a shared list of place names, write that list first, then split the work.

6.3 One prompt, three audiences



Ask your coding assistant

Run three sub-agents in parallel, one per item (none? do the items in turn). Each reads london.qmd, data/ and images/, hides code, follows AGENTS.md and only writes its own files: no rendering.
1. london-dashboard.qmd (format: dashboard): Attractions page (value boxes: top attraction, total `visits_2025`, number free; Plotly bars by attraction; a Plotly line of visits by `year` from data/visits.csv; end each chart cell with `fig`, assigning `fig = fig.update_layout(…)`); Churches page (data/churches.csv, names linked to `visit_london`).
2. london-email.qmd: docx partner brief (2025 numbers as inline code, five sights with official links, getting around, sources); london-email-message.md: its covering email in a text block, no numbers.
3. london-flyer.qmd: one A5 Typst page (papersize: a5): Big Ben photo, five sights with price band and nearest tube, local tip.
Then render the three .qmd files yourself, one at a time, and check each.



Expect it to run

You do

The lead’s renders are uv run quarto render london-dashboard.qmd, then london-email.qmd, then london-flyer.qmd, and it reports each sub-agent’s progress as it goes. The prompt is long because it is three specifications in one, each as concrete as a single prompt would be. The lead checks each file it renders; the office’s checks are yours. Open each output as its reader would: can a manager find the top attraction without reading a sentence, can a partner forward the brief and its email as they are, and does the flyer fit on one A5 page?


Pause and think


A partner asks for this year’s total visits in the covering email itself. Where should the number go, and why?



Answer

In the brief, as inline code, with the email pointing to it. The email is a plain Markdown file that is never rendered, so a number typed there is a copy that will not follow the data.

“End each chart cell with fig” is there because of a failure seen in practice: a Plotly chart appears twice in a dashboard card when the cell both calls fig.show() and returns the figure. Assign the figure, end the cell with its name, and nothing else. If a chart’s legend looks clipped, ask for a horizontal legend with a fixed entrywidth; if the flyer spills onto a second page, ask for a smaller photo.

Paste the prompt and approve the renders.
