6.4 A square advert (optional)



Ask your coding assistant

Create london-social.qmd: one 12 cm square Typst page (raw Typst page size) for social media: "Visit London", the Big Ben photo, the top attraction and its `visits_2025`. Hide code, follow AGENTS.md, render it, and check that the PDF is one square page.


Typst has no square paper name, so the page size is set in a raw Typst block, which Quarto passes to Typst untouched. The finished advert’s photo runs to the edges, so its page has no margin:
```{=typst}
#set page(width: 12cm, height: 12cm, margin: 0cm,
          numbering: none, fill: rgb("#0b2545"))
#set text(fill: white)
```






Figure 6.4: The finished square advert, styled as a social-media ad: a full-bleed photo under an inset border, a gradient that keeps the text legible and a gold call to action. Rendered from examples/london/london-social.qmd.



Everything on the page is placed by raw Typst: the photo fills the square (fit: "cover"), a rectangle with a navy gradient darkens its lower half, and place() positions the border, the text and the badge. The facts are still computed. A Python cell reads attractions.csv and prints them as Typst variables (#let top-name = "Natural History Museum"), which the layout uses, so a corrected count reaches the advert at the next render like every other output.
The finished advert has no title and no level-1 heading: either would land on a page of the default size before the square one. This was tested with Quarto 1.10.20 and its bundled Typst on 2026-11-12. A raw block is a useful escape hatch, and a costly one: it ties the source to one format, so use it only for what the format’s settings cannot express.
If the advert will not come out as one square page, skip it: nothing later depends on it. The finished version is ../quarto-workshop/examples/london/london-social.qmd, which you can copy into your folder and render.

6.5.1 Asking for three.js
You do not need to know three.js to ask for it. Name the library, the data and what you want to do with the result, and check the numbers:



Ask your coding assistant

Create visits-3d.html with `three.js` from a CDN: a labelled 3-D bar per `attraction` in data/visits.csv, as tall as its `visits` in the latest `year`, that I can drag to turn. Put the numbers in the page so it opens by double-click, then check them against the CSV.

three.js is a free JavaScript library (MIT License) that draws 3-D scenes with WebGL, the browser’s built-in 3-D graphics, so the reader installs nothing. Two details of the prompt matter. It asks for the numbers to be written into the page, because a page opened by double-click cannot read local files. And the page loads three.js from a content delivery network (CDN), so it needs the internet to work; a published page keeps that dependency, which is why this book, like the workshop’s slides, ships its own copy of the library.

A 3-D chart has to earn its third dimension. Perspective makes bars harder to compare than a plain bar chart: the near bar looks taller than an equal bar behind it. Figure 5.2 is the better chart for comparing visits. Use 3-D when the third dimension means something, as height does on a map, or for delight, and say which.

title: 7  Publishing and Proving the Rebuild
text:
7.1 Git: every change, safely
The guide is finished, and nobody but you can see it: every output sits in a folder on your computer. This chapter puts it on the web, where anyone can open it on a phone, with Git to keep every version of the source and GitHub Pages to serve the result. Then it asks the question the whole workflow is built to answer: if one input changes, which outputs change with it, and how do you know? That question comes with no prompt. It tests whether you can predict what a rebuild will do, and then check.
Section 1.4 likened Git to Word’s Track Changes for a whole folder, with a lasting history. In practice that means two things. You see exactly what changed, line by line, and someone else can approve it before it counts. And every earlier version of the whole project is kept, with a note saying why it changed, so any of them can be restored or compared.
The vocabulary is short (Figure 7.1; Pro Git and GitHub’s documentation, checked 2026-10-31). A repository is a project folder with its history; each saved version is a commit, a snapshot of every tracked file with its message.
A branch is a movable label on a line of commits, so work can go on there while the main line, main, keeps working. To push is to copy commits to the shared repository on GitHub, the website that keeps a copy of a repository online. A pull request proposes merging a branch and shows the difference, or diff, line by line; a review comments on it, approves it or asks for changes; merging adds its commits to main.
Working alone, as in this book, you commit straight to main and push; in a team, every change goes round the loop. Either way the assistant runs the Git commands and you approve them. Ask it to “commit with a message that says why”, and read its diffs before you approve: a diff is the clearest check you have of what the assistant actually did.

text:
7.2 Where a site lives
A rendered Quarto website is static: a folder of HTML, CSS, JavaScript, images and documents, with no program running on a server. Any web server can serve it, so publishing means copying that folder to a host. GitHub Pages is the host this book uses, because the repository is already on GitHub and quarto publish gh-pages is built in (Figure 7.2).






Figure 7.2: Publishing to GitHub Pages. The source goes to the main branch with Git; quarto publish gh-pages renders the site on your computer and pushes only the rendered HTML to a separate branch, which GitHub serves.



There are two ways to get a site onto a host. Either you render on your own computer and upload the result, as quarto publish does for GitHub Pages and Netlify, or the host builds the site from your repository on every push. The second works only if the build installs Quarto, Python and every package the project needs, or if the rendered output is committed. The London repository leaves its rendered _site/ folder out, so a host that builds would produce nothing until the build is set up.


Pause and think


You connect london-guide to a host that builds from Git, and it publishes an empty site. Why?



Answer

The repository holds no rendered site, because .gitignore leaves _site/ out, and the host’s build has no Quarto, Python or packages unless you install them in it. Either render on your computer and upload the result, or set up the build.

Its README is the first thing visitors to the repository see, and its link takes them on to the live site.
The first publish is yours, typed in the terminal. Stop the preview first: the publish renders the whole site, and two renders in one folder collide. It asks one question, “Publish site … (Y/n)”, which Enter answers yes; then it renders the site, creates the gh-pages branch, pushes the rendered site and opens it. Quarto’s GitHub Pages guide says to run quarto publish gh-pages locally, once, before setting up a GitHub Action to publish (checked 2026-11-12). In that dry run, the first publish of each site took one and a half to two minutes, and GitHub Pages then built it in 20 to 35 seconds, so a 404 page in the first minute usually means the site is still being deployed.

A push that fails with HTTP 400 (“RPC failed”, “the remote end hung up unexpectedly”) was seen with larger sites, such as dashboards with embedded maps. Raise Git’s buffer for this repository with git config http.postBuffer 524288000, and push again.

text:
7.5 Change one input, explain the rebuild
Chapter 1 began with a correction (Section 1.1): ALVA revises one figure, and in a copy-and-paste workflow someone has to carry it by hand into every file that quotes it. Here is that scenario for real, in a project where no visitor count was ever copied. No prompt is supplied: write your own, or do it by hand. Make the edit to the data yourself, for example with nano data/attractions.csv (Ctrl+O, Enter, Ctrl+X): the project’s rules keep the assistant out of data/, which is the point of them.






ImportantTry it




Predict. Set the Tower of London’s visits_2025 in data/attractions.csv to 8000000. Which outputs will change? Write it down before you read on.
Rebuild: stop the preview, then run uv run quarto render.
Explain which outputs changed, which did not, and why.
Undo with git restore data/attractions.csv, then rebuild.


You’re done when you can name the outputs that changed, the ones that did not, and the line of code that links each changed output to the input.

WarningCommon pitfall



Three traps, all met while building the example. The paper’s settings need Quarto 1.10 or newer: Quarto 1.6.40’s Typst rejects them with “unexpected argument: spacing”. An inline expression in a YAML abstract runs before the setup cell and fails, so the finished example writes its abstract in the body, in a raw Typst block. And Typst prints its own heading above the reference list, “Bibliography” by default, which the prompt changes with #set bibliography(title: [References]) so the paper needs no References heading of its own.


A genuine LaTeX PDF is also available, as format: pdf, but it needs a TeX distribution, for example quarto install tinytex. For most reports Typst is faster and simpler.

Git keeps every version as commits; a diff shows what the assistant did.

Answers

ALVA counts only its member sites, so its table is not a list of every London attraction. “London’s most visited attractions” would claim more than the data show (Rules for the guide).
uv.lock, which records the exact version of every package for every system. Their first uv run command, such as uv run quarto render london.md, builds .venv/ from it (An environment for the code to come).
A render writes a temporary notebook named after the file, and the preview was rendering the same file at the same moment, so the two collided. Let the preview do the rendering while it runs, or stop it with Ctrl+C first and restart it afterwards (What a render does, and why two renders collide).
The inline code (the top attraction, its visits and the total) updates at the next render, not when the file is saved. The word “ten” is typed, so it never updates (Numbers the guide computes).
The caption says what the chart is: the measure, the year and whose attractions. The alt text says what it shows, such as which bar is longest and which shortest, for a reader who cannot see it (A chart with a caption and alt text).
No. Both edit the same file, and both are small. Sub-agents suit independent, substantial tasks that write different files; make these two edits in turn (Sub-agents: one lead, many hands).
Typst has a paper name for A5 but none for a 12 cm square, so the advert’s size needs a raw block, which Quarto passes to Typst untouched. A raw block ties the source to one format, so use it only for what the format’s settings cannot express (A square advert (optional)).
Render it yourself and upload it: the pages run Python, and Quarto’s Netlify build plugin runs none. A host that builds would also find no rendered site in the repository, because .gitignore leaves _site/ out (Where a site lives).
The flyer loads no data at all: its facts were copied into its Markdown, so a change to attractions.csv cannot reach it. The live site shows what was last published, and changes only when you publish again (Change one input, explain the rebuild).

The second transfer task compares with 2019 because it is the last year before the pandemic years 2020 and 2021, which data/README.md says are not comparable with the others. The sight to flag is the Natural History Museum: from 2024 its count includes its reopened gardens.

title: Part III: One Analysis, Many Publications
text:
Where Colombia’s tap water is tested, the countryside’s is far riskier than the towns’. In 2023, of the rural zones (a municipality’s countryside, outside its head town) with a utility-supplied water-risk score, 28% fell in the high-risk or unfit bands, against 6% of urban ones. And much rural water has no score at all: that year, 6.8 million of the 12.6 million people in rural zones lived where the open data hold none.
This part asks which kinds of municipal zone exist, judged by water safety, services and context, and how infant mortality, exam scores and school dropout differ between those kinds. Each row of its data is a zone-year: one municipality’s urban zone (the head town) or rural zone in one year. The analysis groups those rows, so a municipality’s two zones can be different kinds. You are the analyst. Your readers are officials, who need a report, and a municipal council, which needs slides, and both deserve an answer that says plainly what the data cannot show:

8  The Question, the Data and the Rules pins down what is asked, what the data mean and what the assistant may not do.
9  Look Before You Model finds where the data are empty or misleading, and meets Tunja, the municipality this part follows.
10  From Table to Features turns the table into features a clustering can use, and counts the cost.
11  Finding Kinds of Places: k-Means lets an algorithm group the zone-years, and decides how many groups there are.
12  Interpreting Clusters names the kinds and compares their outcomes.
13  Correlation Is Not Causation asks whether worse water goes with more infant deaths, and why that is not a cause.
14  Publish Many turns one set of results into a report, slides, a blog post and a website.

The exercises at the end of the part test whether you can do it without the prompts.



Where we are: Part III.

title: 8  The Question, the Data and the Rules
text:
8.1 The question and its readers
In 2023, Colombia’s national report on drinking water scored the water of its urban areas at 5.7, in the low-risk band, and the water of its rural areas at 36.5, in the high-risk band (Table 8.1). DANE’s projections put 12.6 million people, 24% of the population, in rural zones in 2023. People drink and cook with this water, so where the risk sits, and what goes with it, is worth knowing.
The question for this part is therefore: which kinds of municipal zone exist in Colombia, judged by water safety, services and context, and how do health and education outcomes differ between them? Part II’s numbers were simple counts; these are not. Every step has a way to go wrong that a clean render will not reveal: a variable that means something narrower than its name, a gap that is not random, a comparison that looks causal and is not.
The question splits in two, and the order matters:
“Kinds” will be clusters: groups of zone-years, each one municipality’s urban or rural zone in one year (Section 8.4), that are similar to each other on the chosen variables, found by an algorithm called k-means (Chapter 11). Because the unit is a zone in a year, a municipality’s two zones can belong to different kinds, and a zone can move between kinds over the years.
The answer has two readers. Officials will read it as a report, in Word or as a PDF, and a municipal council will see it as a short deck of slides (Chapter 14). Both will look for where to act, and both will be tempted to read a difference between kinds as an effect of the water. So the limits are stated now, each with its reason. The water score covers only systems run by a utility (Section 8.2). Many rural zones have no score at all, so the results describe sampled systems (Section 9.2). And the comparisons describe; they cannot establish that water causes any outcome (Chapter 13).

8.2 Scoring water risk: the IRCA
Colombia scores the safety of drinking water with the IRCA, the Índice de Riesgo de la Calidad del Agua para consumo humano (water-quality risk index for human consumption), defined in Resolución 2115 of 2007. It runs from 0, every test passed, to 100, every test failed, and article 15 sorts the scale into five bands (Table 8.1).

The national average sits in the medium band and hides the urban–rural gap, which is why this part’s data keep each municipality’s two zones apart.






NoteWhy this works



Surveillance samples of tap water are tested against health limits. Each tested characteristic carries a risk score: Escherichia coli 25, total coliforms 15, turbidity 15, free residual chlorine 15, apparent colour 6 and pH 1.5, among others. A sample’s IRCA is the score of the characteristics that fail their limit, as a percentage of the score of all those tested, and a month’s IRCA is the mean over its samples (articles 13 and 14). That is why 0 means every test passed and 100 means every test failed.








WarningCommon pitfall



The IRCA in this part’s data is not the national figure. The open table it comes from (INS, datos.gov.co nxt2-39c3) holds the utility-supplied (“prestadores”) IRCA: samples from systems run by a water utility. A check on 2026-10-30, recorded in the data’s README (caveat 1), found that its 2023 department totals match INCA’s utility column in 30 of 30 departments and the overall figure in only 5. Self-supplied systems, which have no utility, score far worse (43.7 against 7.4 in 2023), so the data understate the risk wherever people rely on self-supply, and say nothing where no utility exists. Label the variable “utility-supplied IRCA” everywhere it appears.

title: 8  The Question, the Data and the Rules
section: 8.3 Saber 11, and what an average covers
text:
8.3 Saber 11, and what an average covers
One of the outcomes the analysis compares (Section 8.5) is an education measure, Saber 11, the national exam taken by students finishing upper secondary school, set by ICFES. It has five tests: critical reading, mathematics, social studies and citizenship, natural sciences, and English. The global score is five times the weighted mean of the five test scores (each 0 to 100; English counts once, the others three times), from 0 to 500, and its mean was fixed at 250 in the first sitting in 2014, so that years can be compared (ICFES, Guía de orientación Saber 11.° 2017-1, pp. 101 and 104, checked 2026-10-30).
Both measures are averages, and an average describes only what it averaged over. IRCA is an average over the water samples taken, so a system that is never sampled has no IRCA at all. The Saber 11 mean in the data is an average over the students who sat the exam at schools in that municipality and zone, so it says nothing about students who had left school. Keep both facts in mind in every comparison that follows.

title: 8  The Question, the Data and the Rules
text:
8.4 Where the data come from
Most of the data are Colombian open data from five public bodies; rainfall and altitude come from two scientific datasets. All are joined on one code: joining two tables matches their rows by a column they share, here the code that DANE’s list of municipalities, DIVIPOLA (División Político-Administrativa), gives each municipality. It has five digits, two for the department and three for the municipality, so 05001 is Medellín, in Antioquia (05). The sources are:

INS (Instituto Nacional de Salud): the IRCA surveillance results.
DANE (the national statistics office): the list of municipalities and their codes, population projections and municipal boundaries.
ICFES and MEN (the Ministry of Education): Saber 11 results and school dropout rates.
DNP (the National Planning Department), through its TerriData portal: water and sewer coverage, multidimensional poverty, municipal performance, transfers for water and infant mortality.
CHIRPS (the Climate Hazards Center’s rainfall data) and NASA SRTM (elevation data): rainfall, and a derived altitude for each head town.

They arrive as three files, in examples/water/data/ in the workshop repository: water_municipal.csv (the analysis table), municipios.geojson (municipal boundaries for maps) and README.md, which documents every column, source, licence and caveat (Appendix G lists them all).
One row is one municipality’s urban or rural zone in one year, a zone-year: this is the analysis’s unit. The urban zone is the head town (cabecera municipal); the rural zone is the smaller settlements and the dispersed countryside. The table covers every one of DANE’s 1,122 DIVIPOLA entries, both zones and every year from 2010 to 2023: 31,416 rows and 29 columns. Of those entries, 1,103 are municipalities; the rest are the island of San Andrés and areas that are not municipalities, whose rows are mostly empty. Because every municipality has all its rows, a gap is an empty cell, never a missing row.


Pause and think


A municipality’s rural zone has no IRCA in one year. Was its water safe that year?



Answer

The data cannot say. IRCA averages the samples taken from utility-run systems, so an empty cell means no utility-supplied score was published: the zone may not have been sampled, or its water may be self-supplied, which nationally scores far worse (Table 8.1). An empty IRCA is unknown, never safe and never zero.








TipIn practice



Read data/README.md before you analyse anything, and ask the assistant to read it first too. Its caveats are the analysis’s traps, written down: the IRCA source above; department capitals that have no urban and rural split for coverage; a fiscal index whose method changes in 2020; infant mortality whose method changes in 2017; Saber 11 only in some years; pesos that are not adjusted for inflation. Each one turns up in the chapters that follow.

title: 8  The Question, the Data and the Rules
text:
8.5 Features and outcomes
The most important design decision in Part III is which variables define the kinds and which only describe them.
The features, which the clustering sees, are nine variables about water, people and place, and government. The outcomes, which the analysis only compares, are infant mortality, the Saber 11 score and school dropout (Table 8.2, Table 8.3). Three features need a word. The multidimensional poverty index (IPM, Índice de Pobreza Multidimensional) is the share of a zone’s people who are poor in several respects at once, from the 2018 census. MDM (Medición de Desempeño Municipal) is DNP’s score of a municipality’s management and results. And SGP (Sistema General de Participaciones) is the system of national transfers to municipalities: the feature is its allocation for drinking water and basic sanitation, per person.
Both tables give each variable’s level and years, computed from the municipalities’ rows. A zone variable differs between a municipality’s urban and rural rows; a municipal one is the same on both; “one value” is repeated every year. Meanings, units and sources come from data/README.md (TerriData is DNP’s data portal).

The last column matters in every chapter that follows. A zone variable is measured separately for a municipality’s urban and rural zones; a municipal one is a single value for the whole municipality, repeated on both of its rows. Five of the nine features are municipal, so a municipality’s two rows in a year differ only in the other four. And a municipal outcome, such as infant mortality, must be counted once per municipality, not once per row.
Never cluster on an outcome. If infant mortality helped define the kinds, the kinds would differ in infant mortality by construction, and the comparison in the second question would be circular: it would find exactly what was put in. Keeping outcomes out of the clustering is what lets the comparison say anything at all.


Pause and think


A colleague wants infant mortality added to the features, “since it is what we care about”. What would the comparison of outcomes between the kinds then show?

That the kinds differ in infant mortality, which would be true by construction: the algorithm would have grouped zones partly by that very number. The comparison would find what was put in. Infant mortality stays an outcome, compared only after the kinds are found.

The same care is why the fiscal index idf is not a feature, although it describes municipal government: its method changes in 2020 (idf to 2020, idf_new from 2020, on different scales), so it cannot form one series across the years the analysis uses. 8.6 Compute once, publish many
Part II computed in each page. Part III computes once (Figure 8.1). One importable script, scripts/analysis.py, does all of the computation and writes its results to outputs/; every page only reads those results and draws them. A design choice, such as how many rows to drop for missing values, is made in one place, and every output follows at the next render.






Figure 8.1: Compute once, publish many. One script turns the data into results once; every publication reads the results, and none recomputes them.



The split solves two problems from Part II. A slow computation no longer slows every page and every format, because it runs once. And no page can disagree with another, because there is only one result to disagree with. Results are saved as Parquet, which keeps column types (a code such as 05001 stays text instead of becoming the number 5001), and as CSV where people will open them.
This book follows the same rule: every number in Part III is computed when the book is built, by importing the finished project’s analysis.py and running it in memory.

9.1 What exploring is for
Before any model, look at the data. Exploring tells you what a model will and will not be able to see: which columns are sparse, which zones are never measured, and whether a series changes level for reasons that have nothing to do with the thing it measures. None of that shows up as an error. A clustering algorithm will happily group rows that have been made comparable only by filling their gaps, and a chart of a series whose method changed will draw a trend that is not there.
The water data hold two such surprises that a chart can show, and several more that show only up close, in one place. For those, this chapter meets Tunja, the municipality the rest of the part follows.
Four questions are worth answering before modelling any table, and this chapter asks each of them of the water data:
The answers decide what the analysis can claim. If one group is mostly missing, conclusions about it rest on the minority that was measured, and that minority may not be typical.

How big is it? Rows and columns, and what one row is.
What is missing, and where? Missingness by column and by group (here, by zone).
How are the key values distributed? For IRCA, the count of rows in each risk band.

text:
9.2 Rural: less data, more risk








Figure 9.1: All rows, 2010–2023, San Andrés and the non-municipalised areas included, by zone: no IRCA reported (hatched) and the Resolución 2115 risk band of the rest. Utility-supplied IRCA, INS open data (datos.gov.co nxt2-39c3).





Side by side, Figure 9.1 shows all 31,416 rows. 53% of rural rows have no IRCA at all, against 14% of urban rows, because many rural systems are never sampled, or are not run by a utility and so fall outside the utility-supplied table. Among the rural rows that do have a value, 51% fall in the high or unfit bands, against 12% of urban rows. Those shares pool all fourteen years. In 2023 alone they were 28% and 6%, the figures that open Part III, after the falls in rural IRCA that Figure 9.2 shows below.
The two facts compound, in the worst direction: the zones whose scores are worse are also the ones least often scored. The gaps are not random. They depend on zone, which the data record, and perhaps on the risk itself, which they do not: statisticians call the second kind missing not at random, and no fill can repair it. Any analysis that drops the rows without IRCA, as Part III’s must, describes sampled rural systems only, and should say so.


Pause and think


Suppose every missing rural IRCA were filled with the median of the scored rural rows. Would rural water then look safer or riskier than it really is?



Answer

Probably safer, though nobody can check. Many unscored systems are ones no utility runs, and self-supplied systems score far worse nationally (Table 8.1), so the fill would turn “unknown, and likely worse” into “typical”. That is why the analysis drops these rows instead (Section 10.1).










Figure 9.2: Median utility-supplied IRCA by year and zone, 2010–2023, over the rows that report one.





The fourth question matters, as Figure 9.2 shows. The rural median drops sharply in 2016 and again in 2020. That could be an improvement in rural water, or a change in which systems were sampled; the data’s README warns that the 2020 drop may reflect sampling, and the open data cannot tell the two apart. An analysis that compares years should not read the drop as progress without evidence from outside the table.
The rural median also ends far below the national rural figure in Table 8.1: 13.4 in 2023, in the low band, against INCA’s 36.5. Two things explain the gap. The table holds only utility-run systems (Section 8.2), and a median of zones is the middle zone, which the worst zones do not pull up, and which is not weighted by how many people drink the water.

title: 10  From Table to Features
text:
10.1 Four steps from table to features
A clustering algorithm does not read a table the way a person does. It sees numbers, measures distances between rows, and groups rows that are close. Everything about the result depends on which rows it sees, which numbers, on what scale, and what it is given where a number is missing. Preparation is the name for those decisions, and they shape the clusters as much as the algorithm does. Four of them stand between the water table and the clustering, and each has a price, counted in rows and in guesses.
1. Select. Keep the years 2016 to 2023, because the municipal performance index (MDM), one of the features, starts in 2016. Keep municipalities only: San Andrés has none of DNP’s values and the non-municipalised areas are nearly empty. Keep only rows with an IRCA value, since water safety is the point of the analysis. IRCA is the one feature never filled: its gaps may depend on the risk itself (Section 9.2), so a filled score would be a guess at exactly what the analysis is about.
2. Transform. Transfers for water per person (SGP) are heavily skewed: most are moderate and a few are very large. So the analysis uses their logarithm, which measures ratios rather than differences: every doubling of a transfer adds the same amount, and the few very large transfers no longer sit far from all the rest. Department capitals have no urban and rural split for coverage, so their urban rows use the municipality’s total coverage instead, and a flag column records that they did. The total suits the urban row because most of a capital’s people live in its head town (88% in the median capital in 2023). It would not suit the rural row: in other municipalities the total exceeds the rural figure in 86% of rural zone-years, so the capitals’ rural rows are filled in the next step instead.
3. Impute, with flags. To impute is to fill a missing value with an estimate. Drop rows missing more than two of the nine features. Fill the remaining gaps with the median of the same year and zone, and add a flag column, such as water_coverage_imputed, that marks every filled value. The median, because a few extreme values cannot pull it; the same year and zone, because rural and urban zones differ (Section 9.2) and years shift.
4. Standardise within each year. Replace each feature by its z-score within its year:
\[z = \frac{x - \bar{x}_{\text{year}}}{s_{\text{year}}}\]
where \(x\) is a row’s value of the feature, and \(\bar{x}_{\text{year}}\) and \(s_{\text{year}}\) are the feature’s mean and standard deviation over that year’s kept rows. The standard deviation is, roughly, the typical distance of a value from the mean, in the feature’s own unit. A z-score of +1 means one standard deviation above that year’s average; a z-score has no unit.

title: 10  From Table to Features
text:
NoteWhy this works



Why within each year rather than over all years? Two reasons. SGP is in nominal pesos, not adjusted for inflation, so its values drift upwards over time for reasons unrelated to any municipality. And other features shift as a whole from year to year, as rural IRCA does in Figure 9.2. Standardising within each year removes both shifts. A zone is compared only with that year’s other zones, so a nationwide shift, real or an artefact of sampling, does not move it between clusters, and one clustering over all years gives labels that mean the same relative position in every year. The price is that a real improvement shared by every zone is invisible to the clusters too.








WarningCommon pitfall



Every fill is a guess, and an unflagged guess becomes indistinguishable from data. The flags make the guesses countable and checkable later: a cluster made mostly of imputed values would be a cluster of medians, not of places. The data’s README says it of the capitals’ coverage (“Do not do it silently”), and the project’s AGENTS.md, written from that README, carries its caveats to the assistant: nothing is filled silently.

title: 10  From Table to Features
text:
10.3 Why scale?
k-means groups rows by straight-line, or Euclidean, distance: the square root of the sum of squared differences across the features. A feature’s share of the expected squared distance, between two rows picked at random, is proportional to its variance, the square of its standard deviation. In raw units, the features measured in thousands, such as millimetres of rain and metres of altitude, dwarf those measured from 0 to 100 (Figure 10.1).








Figure 10.1: Each feature’s share of the squared distance between rows, in raw units (SGP as its logarithm) and after z-scores. Kept rows, 2016–2023.





Unscaled, rainfall and altitude together would make up 99.8% of the distance, so the clusters would be climate zones and the water variables would hardly count. After z-scores, every feature has variance 1 and contributes the same share, about 11%. The log of SGP matters too. In raw pesos, its variance would be about 3,100 times rainfall’s, so it would dominate even rainfall; after z-scores, the log keeps a few very large transfers from sitting far from every other row, cutting the largest z-score from 7.3 to 4.3.
Two real rows show what scaling changes (Table 10.2): the urban zones of Tunja, high in the Andes, and Cartagena, on the Caribbean coast, in 2023. Both are capitals, so their coverage is each municipality’s total. In raw units, their difference in altitude makes up 98% of their squared distance, and a 43-point gap in piped-water coverage makes up less than 1%. In z-scores, coverage counts for 16%, and altitude still leads, at 68%, because height is where the two towns really differ most. Scaling does not make every difference count the same; it stops the units from deciding.

Pause and think


Suppose rainfall were recorded in metres instead of millimetres. What would happen to its share of the distance, unscaled and after z-scores?



Answer

Unscaled, its values would shrink a thousandfold and its variance a millionfold, so its share would all but vanish and altitude would dominate alone. After z-scores nothing would change: the unit cancels, because a z-score divides a distance from the mean by the standard deviation, both in the same unit.








TipIn practice



Equal weight is itself a choice, not a neutral default. Nine z-scored features count equally, so the three safety-and-coverage variables count for 33% of the distance and context for the rest. Equal weight per feature is not equal weight per idea, either: water and sewer coverage are strongly correlated (r = 0.77 over the kept rows, where the correlation coefficient r runs from −1 to 1 and 1 would mean they rise together along a straight line), so what they share counts twice. If water safety should weigh more, that is a decision to make explicitly and report, not to leave to the units the data happened to come in.

title: 11  Finding Kinds of Places: k-Means
text:
11.1 k-means in four steps
The water data now have 11,235 prepared rows, each described by nine z-scores. Nobody can read that many rows. Clustering turns them into a few kinds that a person can name, compare and act on: these municipal zones are like each other, and unlike those. An official can ask which kinds need which help; a council can see which kind its own zones belong to. Clustering needs no labels, so it is a first look at data nobody has categorised, and an odd cluster can point to a data error or a special case. What it cannot do is explain: clusters describe, they do not show causes.
If the mathematics sounds daunting, it need not be. The algorithm is simple enough to watch step by step, and the judgement it needs, how many kinds to look for, is a decision you can write down and check before seeing the answer.
k-means needs one number up front: \(k\), how many clusters to find. It makes one start, then repeats two moves until they change nothing:
Neither move ever raises the inertia, the sum of squared distances from each point to its centre,
\[\text{inertia} = \sum_{i} \lVert x_i - c_{\ell(i)} \rVert^2 ,\]
where \(x_i\) is point \(i\) (for the water data, a row’s nine z-scores), \(c_{\ell(i)}\) is the centre it is assigned to, and \(\lVert x_i - c_{\ell(i)} \rVert\) is the straight-line distance between them (Section 10.3). On z-scores, inertia is in squared standard deviations, a unit with no everyday meaning, so only its changes matter. There are only finitely many ways to group the points, so the algorithm always stops. It does not always stop at the best answer: a bad start can trap it in a worse grouping. Figure 11.1 shows the algorithm on 560 synthetic points in three groups, which are toy data made up for the illustration, not the water data.
Figure 11.2: The same algorithm on the toy points, flattened to two of their three dimensions: the random start, the first assignment, an assignment halfway, and the stable result.
Different starts can end in different groupings, so the real analysis runs k-means from 20 starts (scikit-learn’s n_init) and keeps the one with the lowest inertia. The starts are random, but repeatable: a fixed random seed, the number that starts the computer’s random-number generator, makes them the same on every run, so your project, the deck and this book all get the same clusters.

NoteWhy this works



The real starts are not dropped at random, as in the toy. scikit-learn’s default, k-means++ (Arthur and Vassilvitskii, 2007), picks the first centre at random from the data and each next one with probability proportional to its squared distance from the nearest centre already chosen. text:
11.2 Choosing k
k is a hyperparameter: a setting the algorithm cannot learn from its own objective, because inertia always falls as k grows, down to zero when every point is its own cluster. So the analysis fits k-means for k from 2 to 8 and reads two measures (Figure 11.3). The first is where inertia stops falling much, the elbow. The second, the silhouette, scores from −1 to 1 how much closer each point is to its own cluster than to the next one, averaged over the points. It needs every distance between points, so it is computed on a fixed sample of 5,000 rows, which keeps it fast.








Figure 11.3: Choosing k: inertia and silhouette for k = 2 to 8, fitted on all kept rows. The chosen k is marked.





The rule, written into choose_k() in the analysis script, has three parts, and Table 11.1 applies it row by row:

k = 2 is excluded. Two clusters mostly split urban from rural rows, which we knew already: they match the zone for 86% of rows. The script measures this with the adjusted Rand index (ARI), which scores how far two groupings agree beyond what chance would give: 1 means identical, 0 no better than chance. Here it is 0.50.
The elbow: take the smallest k from 3 up after which one more cluster cuts inertia by less than 10%. Here that is k = 4: a fifth cluster cuts inertia by only 7%.
The silhouette check: k’s silhouette must be within 0.01 of the best for k ≥ 3. At k = 4 it is 0.195. The check rules out only k = 8 here.

The elbow is marginal. The fourth cluster itself cuts inertia by 10.8% (the row for k = 3), only just above the 10% threshold, so a threshold of 11% would pick k = 3 instead. And the four clusters account for 41% of the spread in the data, one minus the ratio of their inertia to that of a single cluster; the rest is difference within the kinds.
Two more checks follow the fit. Stability: refits from 5 other seeds agree, with an adjusted Rand index of at least 0.998, so the result does not depend on the start. That says nothing about other data, features or k; refitting on rows drawn again at random (a bootstrap), or leaving out one year at a time, would test that. Ordering: clusters are numbered by their centre’s IRCA, from lowest to highest, so a re-run keeps the same numbers and colours.






WarningCommon pitfall



A silhouette near 0.2 is low. In the subjective reading Rousseeuw and colleagues propose, a best average silhouette of 0.25 or less means that “no substantial structure has been found” (Struyf, Hubert and Rousseeuw, 1997, Table 2), and the best here, at any k, is 0.24. The kinds overlap: they summarise a continuum rather than separate islands of data. So treat k as a judgement call, and do not force a number of clusters to make a nicer story. Writing the rule down before seeing the result is what keeps such a choice honest; choose_k() at least makes the rule explicit, so anyone can check it and see how close the call was.




Pause and think


An official reads the report and asks: “So Colombia has four kinds of municipal zone?” What do you answer?



Answer

That four is a useful summary, not a discovery. A written rule chose it by a narrow margin, and a threshold one percentage point higher picks three; the low silhouette says the kinds overlap. The clusters describe typical combinations of water, services and context, and a zone near the edge of one could as well sit in the next.

11.3 A picture of the clusters
Nine dimensions cannot be drawn. Principal component analysis (PCA) finds the directions in which the data vary most and projects the rows onto them. Each direction, a principal component, is a weighted sum of the nine z-scores, and its weights, called loadings, say what it measures. Figure 11.4 uses the first two components, which keep 30% and 21% of the variance.








Figure 11.4: Each dot is a zone-year on the first two principal components of the nine z-scored features, coloured and shaped by cluster. PCA is only for the picture: k-means used all nine features.





Overlaps in the picture can be separations in the dimensions it leaves out. Adding a third component, which keeps another 16% of the variance, shows how much (Figure 11.5). On two components, on average 78% of a zone-year’s 15 nearest neighbours are in its own cluster; on three, 94%. The third component rises with altitude and falls with rainfall, its two largest loadings. Cluster 3, the most mixed in two dimensions, sits below the others along it: it is the lowest and wettest of the kinds.

title: 12  Interpreting Clusters
text:
12.1 What sets each cluster apart
Cluster 4 is a number, and a number is hard to act on. “Rural, low-coverage, high-risk water” is a phrase an official can repeat and a council can argue over, and anyone can check it, provided a rule produced it rather than someone’s eye. The names carry most weight in the comparison the analysis was built for: infant mortality, exam scores and school dropout, which the clustering never saw, kind by kind. That comparison is where readers draw conclusions, so it is where honesty matters most, and it gets three views, because each hides something the others show.
A cluster’s profile is the mean of each feature over its rows, in z units (Section 10.1): +1 means one standard deviation above that year’s average across all kept rows (Figure 12.1). Read along a cluster’s line to describe it, and along a feature’s line to see which feature separates the clusters.
Figure 12.1: Cluster profiles in z units: standard deviations above (red) or below (blue) the year’s average. IRCA: utility-supplied. Altitude: derived SRTM point.
The highest-IRCA cluster, cluster 4, stands out on three things at once: piped-water coverage (−1.3 SD), poverty (+1.0 SD) and IRCA (+0.8 SD). Each cluster is such a combination, which is exactly what a single variable could not have found.

12.2 Name them by a rule
Names make clusters usable, and they also make them persuasive, so they need a rule that anyone can check. The analysis script’s name_rule() builds each name from three parts:

Setting, tested in this order: “Rural” if fewer than 40% of the cluster’s rows are urban zones; otherwise “Cities and large towns” if its rural share is 0.5 SD or more below average, “Lowland towns” if its altitude is 0.5 SD or more below, “Highland towns” if 0.5 SD or more above, and plain “Towns” if none of these holds.
Coverage: “low-coverage” if the cluster’s mean piped-water coverage is 0.5 SD or more below average.
Risk: the Resolución 2115 band of the cluster’s median utility-supplied IRCA, the middle value when its zone-years are sorted by IRCA.

12.3 Where Tunja lands
The cluster that holds all 16 of Tunja’s zone-years, urban and rural, now has a name: cluster 1 (cities and large towns), “Cities and large towns, no-risk water”. For the urban zone, it fits. For the rural zone, the label hides most of what Section 9.3 found. Its water scored in the high-risk band every year from 2010 to 2014, before the analysis’s window opens in 2016, and inside the window its utility-supplied IRCA is never in the no-risk band, and is in the medium band in three of the eight years.
Two things are at work. The risk word describes the cluster’s median, not each member, as Section 12.2 warned. And k-means puts each zone-year in the cluster whose centre is nearest over all nine features at once (Section 11.1), adding up the squared differences feature by feature. Table 12.2 splits that sum in two. On its own four features, IRCA, piped-water coverage, sewer coverage and poverty, Tunja’s rural zone sits nearer the centre of cluster 4 (rural), and two of those, the coverages, are fills (Section 10.2). 12.4 Outcomes by cluster
Now the outcomes, which the clustering never used (Figure 12.2). Each line is a cluster’s median within each year, so a shift that moves every kind in one year cannot pass for a difference between kinds. Infant mortality is compared only in 2017–2019 and 2021–2023: its method changes in 2017, and 2020 looks like another source (the data’s README, caveat 8).








Figure 12.2: Median outcome by cluster and year: infant mortality in 2017–2019 and 2021–2023 only, Saber 11 in its published years. Descriptive only: not causal effects of water safety.





Gaps in the lines are years with no comparable value, drawn as gaps rather than joined across. Infant mortality and dropout are measured for a whole municipality but repeated on both zone rows, so they are counted once per municipality in each cluster and year: for these two the unit is the municipality-year, one municipality in one year, while the features and Saber 11 stay per zone-year.
Figure 12.3 puts the outcomes on the features’ scale: each outcome standardised within its year, a cell being the cluster’s mean z, with the mean itself in brackets.








Figure 12.3: Cluster mean outcome in z units, with the mean in brackets. Red is above average: better for Saber 11, worse for the other two. Descriptive only.





The paleness is the finding. No cluster’s mean outcome is more than 0.65 standard deviations from the average, against 1.32 for the features that formed them: the kinds differ less in outcomes than in what defines them. Part of this is by design: k-means chose the clusters to separate the features, so they should differ more on those than on anything else. Within that: the lowest recorded infant mortality is in cluster 1 (cities and large towns) and the highest in cluster 2 (highland towns); the best Saber 11 scores are in cluster 1 (cities and large towns); and the lowest dropout is in cluster 2 (highland towns).


Pause and think


Suppose unsafe water did harm infants’ health a great deal. Would you still expect the outcome heatmap to be paler than the features’?



Answer

Yes. k-means chose the clusters to separate the features, so they differ most on those by construction. The outcomes differ only as far as they go with the features, and small places’ noisy rates blur them further. Paleness alone is no evidence that water does not matter.


The highest recorded infant mortality is not in the cluster with the worst water, cluster 4 (rural). That is a good moment to slow down rather than to explain it away, because two things in the data push the same way. The first is small numbers. The rates of cluster 2 (highland towns) come from the smallest places of any kind, a median of 10,680 people per municipality-year, where a handful of deaths moves a rate a long way.
The second is what is missing. From 2017 the series looks like observed rates rather than modelled estimates, so a municipality where no infant died that year should show a rate of 0, yet no zero appears anywhere: a blank may be a recorded zero. 50% of this kind’s municipality-years are blank, against 32% of all clustered municipality-years. Leaving the blanks out drops what may be zeros, which raises small places’ averages most. That is selection on the outcome: whether a row is kept depends on the value being measured, so the rows kept are not typical. It may account for part of this kind’s place at the top. Small numbers, reporting and many other differences between the kinds all sit between a cluster’s water and its outcomes, and Chapter 13 takes that up directly.

title: 13  Correlation Is Not Causation
text:
13.1 Worse water, more infant deaths?
The analysis was built to ask whether places with worse water have worse outcomes, and the temptation, once there is a chart, is to read the answer as an effect: worse water causes more infant deaths. The data cannot support that sentence, and this chapter shows why, with the analysis’s own numbers.
One more comparison, the association between water safety and infant mortality within each kind of place, comes out weak in every kind, and in one as large as across all of them. But neither a strong association nor a weak one could settle the causal question here, and the reasons decide how the results must be written. That last part is not a formality: the sentence a reader quotes is the one you publish.
The measure is Spearman’s \(\rho\) (rho), which asks whether two variables rise and fall together in rank order: sort the places by each variable, and see whether the two orders agree. It runs from −1 (perfectly opposite) through 0 to +1 (perfectly together), where 0 means no monotonic relation, one in which a variable tends to rise as the other rises, though not necessarily along a straight line. Because it uses ranks, it is not thrown by extreme values, which matters with small municipalities’ noisy rates.
Across all municipality-years with both values in 2017–2019 and 2021–2023, \(\rho\) between utility-supplied IRCA and infant mortality is +0.10 (n = 4,016, the number of municipality-years compared). Figure 13.1 shows what so weak an association looks like: a cloud with no visible slope.
Figure 13.1: Every municipality-year with both values, 2017–2019 and 2021–2023: utility-supplied IRCA, the mean of its scored zones, against infant mortality (log scale). Descriptive only.
A small positive association across all places could come from water, or from everything that differs between places with safe and unsafe water. The clusters offer a partial control, a way of comparing like with like: within a cluster, places are more alike in poverty, rurality, coverage and altitude than across the country, though far from equal (Table 13.1).

The first is range. The clusters were formed partly on IRCA, so inside clusters 1 and 2 it varies far less than across all places, and inside clusters 3 and 4 more. A narrower range tends to weaken a rank correlation, but that does not explain these four: \(\rho\) is largest in cluster 2, where IRCA varies little, and closest to zero in cluster 4, where it varies most.
The second is chance. That mean is unweighted, and it covers only the zones with a score: in 54% of the pooled municipality-years only one zone has one. So the IRCA beside a rate is one zone’s score or the plain mean of two, not what the average resident drinks.
It would be easy to read this as “water does not matter”. That reading is as unsupported as the first one.

title: 13  Correlation Is Not Causation
text:
13.2 What else could explain it
Figure 13.3 draws the paths between water and infant mortality that the data cannot separate.






Figure 13.3: What else could explain it. The dashed arrow is the question; every other path can create an association without an effect, or hide an effect that exists.



Poverty and rurality are likely confounders. A confounder is a third variable that affects both the exposure, here water safety, and the outcome, here infant deaths, so the two move together even if one has no effect on the other. Poorer, more rural places tend to have less safe water and, for other reasons, more infant deaths, so they can produce an association between water and mortality with no effect of water at all. Health-service access carries part of that path: poorer and remoter places have less of it, and less access means more infant deaths.
Reporting quality is a problem of measurement, and it works the other way: places with weak birth and death registration record fewer infant deaths than occur, and if those are also the places with unsafe water, under-recording can hide a real effect. Blanks add a second problem. The series holds no zeros, so a blank rate may mean no deaths were recorded, and 32% of the clustered municipality-years in these years are blank. Leaving them out drops what may be recorded zeros, which raises small places’ averages most: a selection on the outcome itself (Section 12.4).
Then there is the ecological level. IRCA is measured for an urban or rural zone, infant mortality for the whole municipality. A pattern across places need not hold for the people in them: the infants who died need not be the ones drinking the worst water. Drawing individual conclusions from aggregate data is known as the ecological fallacy.
Tunja shows the mismatch in one place. In this check each of its six municipality-years counts once in cluster 1, with the mean IRCA of its two zones: in 2018, for example, 9.15, halfway between its urban water’s 0.5 and its rural water’s 17.8, a value neither zone had. The mean weighs the two zones equally, though at most 5% of Tunja’s people live in the rural one, and the infant mortality beside it is the whole municipality’s.
The clusters narrow some of these differences without removing them: within a cluster, places still differ in poverty and access (Table 13.1). And small municipalities produce extreme rates, which add noise that flattens any line.


Pause and think


Pick one of these paths. Could it hide a real effect, or create a fake one?



Answer

Poverty can create a fake one: if poorer places tend to have both less safe water and, for other reasons, more infant deaths, the two move together without water doing anything. Reporting quality can hide a real one: if unsafe-water places under-record deaths, their measured rates are too low, and a real effect looks smaller than it is. Only the first is a confounder; the second is a problem of measurement. Each path pushes one way, but several act at once and their sizes are unknown, so the net bias could go either way, which is why a correlation cannot settle the question.

That is a different study, with different data; Hernán and Robins, in Further reading, cover such designs.

13.3 Writing it honestly
Every output of this analysis says the same thing in the same words, because the project’s rules require it: comparisons between clusters are descriptive and do not establish a causal effect of water safety. In practice that means a few habits:

Describe what was compared, and over which rows: “within each cluster, 2017–2019 and 2021–2023, municipality-years with both values”.
Use verbs of association (“is higher in”, “varies with”), not of effect (“raises”, “reduces”, “leads to”).
Name the data’s limits beside the result: the utility-supplied IRCA, the method change in infant mortality, the zone-versus-municipality mismatch.
State what the result does not show, in one sentence a reader could quote.







WarningCommon pitfall



The causal sentence usually arrives in the last step: a slide title, a blog post’s headline, a summary for a council. Ask the assistant to check every title and summary against the project’s rules, and read them yourself. “Utility-supplied water risk (IRCA) and infant mortality in Colombian municipalities” is a fair title; “How unsafe water kills infants” is not, however strongly you suspect it.

title: 13  Correlation Is Not Causation
text:
Summary


Spearman’s \(\rho\) measures whether two variables rise and fall together in rank order; across all places, utility-supplied IRCA and infant mortality are only weakly associated (\(\rho\) = +0.10).
Within the clusters, where places are more alike but far from equal, \(\rho\) runs from −0.04 to +0.10; range, chance and a different unit mean these values cannot be ranked or set beside the pooled one at face value.
Poverty and rurality are likely confounders that can create an association with no effect, while weak reporting and blank rates can hide a real one.
IRCA is measured per zone and infant mortality per municipality, and reading a pattern across places as one about the people in them is the ecological fallacy, as Tunja’s averaged zones show.
Neither a strong nor a weak association settles the causal question; that needs a design, such as before-and-after comparisons with comparable places.
Write about association: name the rows compared, use verbs of association, put the limits beside the result and say what it does not show.

14.1 The report, in Word and PDF
The officials will read the findings as a report, so they need it in the formats offices pass around: Word and PDF. The municipal council will see them on a screen in a meeting, and will look to the last slide for the conclusion. Both will look for where to act, and anyone else needs a link. So the project gets a report, slides and a website with a blog post, and not one of them may compute anything. Each reads outputs/, and that is what makes the chapter’s last test fair: change one setting in the analysis, predict what follows, rebuild, and check that every publication followed.
The prompt lists the report’s sections, and three of its choices carry the lessons of the last chapters. “Utility-supplied” is in the data section because Section 8.2 showed what the label hides. “Correlation ≠ causation” is a section, not a footnote. And the figures are matplotlib, because Word, PowerPoint and PDF cannot run the JavaScript that interactive Plotly charts need (Figure 14.1).
Every number in the text is inline code reading outputs/, never typed: a report that quotes the number of kept rows quotes whatever the analysis last computed. You should have report.html, report.docx and report.pdf, each with the heatmap, the outcomes and the within-cluster figure.

Make this folder a Quarto website: _quarto.yml (execute-dir: project, `pre-render` scripts/analysis.py, freeze: false, render list, navbar), index.qmd listing posts/, and one post titled with the real k, e.g. "Four kinds of municipal zone". Render it; check the links.



You do

uv run quarto preview


The preview’s home page should list one post, whose title states the real k.
The post’s title states the number of clusters, so a change in the analysis could leave it wrong. The finished post protects itself with one line in its setup cell, assert k == 4, which fails the render if the analysis ever finds a different k (Figure 14.3). That line is a guard: it stops the render when a sentence’s words, not only its numbers, no longer match the data, because a loud failure is better than a quiet falsehood. This book guards its own sentences the same way. Section 12.4 says that the highest recorded infant mortality is not in the cluster with the worst water; if new data made that false, the book would stop building rather than print it.






Figure 14.3: The finished blog post, whose title states the number of clusters the analysis found. Rendered from examples/water/posts/four-kinds-of-municipal-zone/index.qmd.




14.4.1 Fresh or frozen?
freeze: false is the simple, safe setting: every render recomputes everything, so nothing can be stale. The cost is time, every render, for every page. freeze: auto is the alternative: Quarto stores each page’s results in _freeze/ and re-executes a page only when its own source changes.
The catch is in that last phrase. Quarto does not know which files a page reads, so a change to data/ or to outputs/ is not detected, and a frozen page keeps its old numbers. With freeze: auto you need a rule for throwing results away: delete _freeze/ (or render that one page directly, which ignores the cache) whenever the data or the analysis change.


Pause and think


Your site uses freeze: auto. You change MAX_MISSING in scripts/analysis.py and run uv run quarto render. Which pages show the new numbers?



Answer

Only pages whose own source changed, and you changed none. pre-render still rewrites outputs/, but every frozen page reuses its stored results, so the site shows the old numbers beside new output files until you delete _freeze/ or render each page on its own.








TipIn practice



Start with freeze: false and switch only when renders become slow enough to matter, and when you do, write the invalidation rule down where the next person will find it. This book uses freeze: auto, so the EPUB rebuilds quickly and reproducibly, and its rule is written in its configuration and README: after any change to the examples’ data or analysis, run make book-fresh, which deletes _freeze/ and re-executes every chapter.

14.7 A dashboard and a white paper (optional)
A dashboard can show the clusters on a map. The first prompt builds a Plotly choropleth, a map whose areas are coloured by a value, here each municipality by its urban zone’s IRCA band, with a year slider; the second adds pages for the kinds, the outcomes and the method:



Ask your coding assistant

Create dashboard.qmd (format: dashboard): a Plotly choropleth of the IRCA band of the "urban" rows of outputs/clusters.parquet on data/municipios.geojson (featureidkey="properties.divipola"), a year slider over their years (frames update only z), an itables table of outputs/clusters.parquet (maxBytes=0); end each chart cell with `fig`. Make it polished: IRCA bands in order from no risk to unfit, light to dark, with a legend, titled cards and readable labels. Add it to the navbar; render, check it looks good at laptop size and report errors.


When the map page looks right, the second prompt adds the other pages:



Ask your coding assistant

Add Kinds, Outcomes and Method pages to dashboard.qmd from outputs/ only: a heatmap of cluster_profiles.csv's `z_` columns; outcomes_by_year.csv medians by `year` and `cluster`, and irca_infant.csv's ρ; k_selection.csv's inertia and silhouette by k. Use each cluster's `color` and axis units; say it is descriptive, not causal. Render; check each page at laptop size.








Figure 14.4: The finished dashboard’s map page. Rendered from examples/water/dashboard.qmd.









WarningCommon pitfall



Three traps, all met building the example. The boundary file follows the GeoJSON standard (exterior rings counter-clockwise) and Plotly expects the opposite, so without reversing the rings every municipality is drawn as “the world minus the municipality”, a grey rectangle; the finished script’s load_geojson() reverses them. Animation frames must update only the colours (z): if every year repeats the 2.7 MB of boundaries, the page balloons. And a dashboard cell shows every top-level expression, not only the last, so a bare fig.add_vline(…) draws the chart twice; assign it, fig = fig.add_vline(…), and end the cell with fig.


The searchable table needs maxBytes=0, or itables silently drops rows to keep the page small.
The same outputs can also become an academic paper, as London’s did (Section 7.6), now with numbered equations ($$ … $$ {#eq-kmeans}, referred to as @eq-kmeans) and citations of the papers behind each method:



Ask your coding assistant

Create whitepaper.qmd from outputs/: A4 Typst, "New Computer Modern"; an abstract (no inline code), numbered Introduction, Methods with equations, Results and Conclusions, then References via `#set bibliography(title: [References])`. Cite data/README.md's sources and the k-means, silhouette and ARI papers in references.bib; open each DOI. Add it to `render` and the "Downloads" menu; render; check equations and citations. Figures must be vector: set `fig-format: svg` and check that the files in `figure-typst/` end in .svg.








WarningCommon pitfall



“Open each DOI” is there for a reason: an assistant can produce a plausible reference that does not exist. A DOI is a document’s permanent identifier, and https://doi.org/ followed by it opens the publisher’s page, so it is a quick test that a reference exists. Ask the assistant to drop any reference it cannot open rather than guess, and check the reference list yourself. The finished paper cites Lloyd (1982) for k-means, Rousseeuw (1987) for the silhouette, Hubert and Arabie (1985) for the adjusted Rand index and Pedregosa et al. (2011) for scikit-learn, each checked against its publisher’s page on 2026-11-01.

14.8 Further challenges
These have no checkpoints. Each extends the analysis with data already in the project, or names one that is not yet available:

Moves between kinds. Count how municipalities’ zones move between clusters from 2016 to 2023, and draw it as a Sankey diagram (Plotly’s go.Sankey).
Positive deviants. Find municipalities whose rural zone is in the high-risk kind yet whose recorded infant mortality is low, and check first whether that is small numbers, blanks or under-registration.
Other clusterings. A Gaussian mixture model gives each row a probability per cluster instead of a hard label; HDBSCAN finds dense groups and leaves outliers unclustered. Do the kinds survive?
A better outcome. Diarrhoeal disease in children under five is the outcome most directly linked to water. Its incidence is not in the open data of SIVIGILA, Colombia’s public-health surveillance system, which publish only deaths; the data’s README records it as a source to add when it becomes available.

title: Exercises for Part III
text:
Answers to the review questions

Because the analysis then compares outcomes between the kinds. If infant mortality helped define them, they would differ in infant mortality by construction, and the comparison would find exactly what was put in (Features and outcomes). Outcomes describe the clusters; they never define them.
The open table holds the IRCA of systems run by water utilities, not the national figure. Self-supplied systems, which have no utility, score far worse (Scoring water risk: the IRCA), so the data understate the risk wherever people rely on self-supply, and say nothing where no utility exists. Without the label, a reader would take the figure for the national one, and think water safer than it is wherever self-supply is common.
They describe sampled rural systems only: those run by a utility and tested. The gaps are not missing at random. They depend on the zone, and perhaps on the risk itself, since the zones least often scored are the riskiest where they are scored, so every rural result should say which systems it covers (Rural: less data, more risk, What the steps keep).
k-means groups rows by straight-line distance, where a feature counts in proportion to its variance. In raw units, rainfall and altitude would decide the clusters on their own, and the kinds would be climate zones. z-scores give every feature the same weight, and computing them within each year removes shifts that move every place at once, such as transfers in pesos not adjusted for inflation, so a cluster means the same relative position in every year (Why scale?, Four steps from table to features).
No, but the kinds overlap: they summarise a continuum rather than separate islands of data. That is why k is chosen by a rule written down before seeing the result, and why the kinds are described, not treated as natural types. Refits from other seeds agree, which shows only that the result does not depend on the start, not that it would survive other data or features (Choosing k).
Right about the kind, wrong about this member: Tunja’s rural water was never in the no-risk band in 2016–2023. The risk word is the band of the cluster’s median IRCA, not a claim about every zone-year in it, and k-means places a row by all nine features, several of which Tunja’s two zones share as one municipality (Name them by a rule, Where Tunja lands). A statement about Tunja needs Tunja’s rows.
Both read a description as an effect. The first turns a difference between kinds into a cause, though poverty, rurality, health-service access and reporting differ between the kinds too. The second reads a weak association as no effect, though weak reporting can hide deaths and small municipalities add noise (What else could explain it). Instead, say what was compared over which rows, with verbs of association, and add one sentence saying the comparison does not establish a causal effect of water safety (Writing it honestly).
The mean weighs the two zones equally, though only a small share of Tunja’s people live in the rural one, and it lies between two values that neither zone had. IRCA is measured per zone and infant mortality per municipality, so a pattern across places need not hold for the people in them; reading it as if it did is the ecological fallacy (What else could explain it).
pre-render re-runs the analysis, which rewrites outputs/, and freeze: false re-executes every page, so every page that reads outputs/ is fresh. The explore page re-runs too, but it reads only data/water_municipal.csv, which did not change (Table 14.1). The live site is the last _site/ you published, and changes only when you publish again (Publish it). With freeze: auto, Quarto would re-execute a page only when its own source changed: it does not see outputs/ or data/, so pages would keep their old numbers until the cache was cleared (A website with a blog).

title: Afterword: What You Built, and Where Next
text:
What you can now do
Near the end of Part III, one setting changed in one script, and the officials’ report, the council’s slides, the blog post and the dashboard all changed with it, without a number retyped. That moment is what the two projects were for. The London guide and the water analysis each started from plain text and data, became a shelf of documents for different readers, and rebuild with one command. The projects will date. The method will not, and it fits on a card.
Part III added four habits that travel to any analysis. Follow one case, your own Tunja, through every step, because aggregates hide what a single place shows. Label each variable for what it measures, as “utility-supplied” did for the IRCA. Never define groups by the outcome you will compare them on. And open every reference an assistant gives you before you cite it.
The formats were never the goal. Work with data, software and AI applications pays off when its audience engages with it and acts on it: a manager decides, a council funds a water supply, a reader tries the method. Quarto, git and a hosting service make that work reproducible, so others can trust it, act on it and build on it; an assistant makes it fast; checking keeps it right. What stays with you is the judgement no tool makes: who the work is for, and what would make them read it.

If one of these is shaky, go back to that part’s exercises, starting from a known-good state in Appendix E — Checkpoints at a Glance, and Answers.

title: Afterword: What You Built, and Where Next
section: Your own project, in three turns
text:
Your own project, in three turns
The order matters more than the tools.

One output, for one reader. Start with the document your readers already ask for, usually a report, in a project folder with its data, kept unchanged, and an AGENTS.md. Prompt for the skeleton; check that it renders and answers the reader’s question.
Make it compute. Replace every typed number with inline code that reads the data, or the results of one analysis script, and guard any sentence whose conclusion depends on them. Check by changing one input in a copy and watching the number move.
Add formats, then readers. Word or a PDF, then slides, then a website, each reading the same results. Check with a prediction: change a setting, say what will change, rebuild and compare. Then publish.

The second format is where the approach starts to repay the setup; the first change to the data is where it pays for itself.
Assistants, models and Quarto’s options will keep changing, and some details in this book with them. The loop does not. Prompt for one thing. Check it against the data. Publish only what you checked, from one source, as often as the data change.

title: Appendix A — Windows: Get Ubuntu Ready

Before you start
This appendix is step 1 of the setup (Section 3.2) for Windows. The workshop’s tools are made for Linux, so on Windows you install Ubuntu, a widely used version of Linux, inside Windows with WSL, the Windows Subsystem for Linux. Think of Windows as your house, with your browser, files and apps, and Ubuntu as a room inside it, a window where you type commands. Everything in this book happens in that room, your Windows browser still opens what you make, and nothing on Windows is removed.
Why not PowerShell, Windows’s own command window? Because the book’s commands, and the way the setup was tested, are for Linux. Some tools have Windows installers, but their paths and commands differ, and each variant is another way to go wrong.
Figure A.1 shows the whole procedure in one window. The steps below go slowly, with a restart in the middle, and the first time Ubuntu opens it also asks you to choose a username and password, which the animation skips.
Do one step, compare your screen with You should see, then go on. If something looks different, see If you are stuck.

title: Appendix B — Terminal Keys and Habits
text:
Habits
A handful of keys make the terminal much faster and less error-prone. They are defaults in Bash, Ubuntu’s shell, and zsh, the Mac’s, and in Windows Terminal and the Mac’s Terminal app (GNU Bash and zsh line-editor manuals; Microsoft and Apple keyboard documentation; all checked 2026-10-31).
Other keys edit the line you are typing, clear the screen or find a command you typed before:
crumbs: Appendices
B  Terminal Keys and Habits

title: Appendix B — Terminal Keys and Habits
text:
Know where you are. Run pwd before starting an assistant: its answer is the assistant’s root folder (Section 2.4).
Two tabs. Keep the assistant in one tab and commands such as quarto preview in another, both in the project folder.
New tab after installing. A terminal learns where programs are when it starts, so a program installed a moment ago is “not found” until you open a new tab.
Read before you run. Whether a command comes from the book, a web chat or the assistant, read it before you press Enter or approve it, especially anything with sudo or rm.
Copy errors whole. When something fails, copy the command and the entire error text; the useful line is rarely the last one.
Edit small files in the terminal. nano AGENTS.md opens a file in a simple editor: Ctrl+O, then Enter, saves it, and Ctrl+X leaves. On a Mac, nano opens Pico, which uses the same keys (checked on macOS 26, 2026-11-12); both list their keys along the bottom of the screen.

title: Appendix E — Checkpoints at a Glance, and Answers
text:
Answer: changing a London input
The task (Section 7.5): set the Tower of London’s visits_2025 to 8,000,000.
What changes. Every page that loads attractions.csv (Table 7.3) is rebuilt with the new count, and what it shows depends on its code. The guide, in every format it writes (web page, Word and PDF, and PowerPoint, slides and EPUB if made), the dashboard’s value boxes and bar chart, and the partner brief (london-email.docx) find the top attraction with idxmax() and the total with .sum(), so the Tower of London becomes the most visited attraction and the total rises. The square advert, if made, uses only idxmax(), so it names the Tower too. The white paper names no top attraction: its sums by admission change, but its table keeps ALVA’s rank_uk column from the file, so it would still rank the Tower ninth in the UK beside the most visits of the ten. A copied column goes stale too.
What does not. The flyer, which copies its facts and quotes no visit counts; the covering email (london-email-message.md), which quotes no numbers and is not rendered; the dashboard’s line chart and the 3-D map, which read visits.csv, not attractions.csv; any output not rebuilt; and the live site, until it is published again.
Why. Every render re-runs every page’s code (freeze: false), and each changed output is linked to the input by a line of code that loads it. A strong answer names that line.
Follow-up questions worth asking. Where would the change appear if the number had been typed into the prose instead of computed? (Nowhere: the typed number would silently disagree with the chart.) What would change if visits.csv were edited instead? (The dashboard’s line chart, the 3-D map and the white paper’s trend.) Why does the render re-run every cell? (Because nothing is cached; see Section 14.4.)
